cards.p: All living things are made of cells, and the cell is the smallest unit of life. In multicellular organisms, cells form a layered order: cell → tissue → organ → system → organism.

cards.h: Metabolism: building up and breaking down
cards.p: All the chemical reactions in a living thing are called metabolism. Building large molecules from small ones is called anabolism, and it uses energy. Breaking down large molecules is called catabolism. Digestion and respiration are examples, and they usually release energy.

cards.key: Metabolism is the sum of anabolism, the building reactions, and catabolism, the breakdown reactions.

cards.p: A cell cannot use the energy in food directly. It first loads this energy onto ATP molecules. When the cell does work, ATP splits into ADP and phosphate. A cell holds only a small amount of ATP, so ATP is made again all the time.

cards.p: Every living thing feeds. Autotrophs make their own food, and heterotrophs take in ready-made food. Through respiration, the energy in food is passed to ATP. Through excretion, wastes such as carbon dioxide and urea are removed from the body.

cards.key: Plants also carry out respiration. Photosynthesis does not replace respiration.

etk.soru: Sort each organism by how it gets food.
ogeler: It has chlorophyll. It makes its own food by photosynthesis.
Fungi have no chlorophyll. They absorb ready-made food from their surroundings.
Yeast is a fungus. It takes in ready-made sugar.

once.soru: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis. Do they also carry out respiration?

secenekler.neden: Photosynthesis makes food, and respiration passes the energy in that food to ATP. Every living plant cell respires, day and night.
To use the energy in the food it makes, a plant must also carry out respiration.
Respiration goes on during the day too. Photosynthesis is faster in daytime, so respiration goes unnoticed.

cards.p: In asexual reproduction, a single parent produces offspring like itself. A bacterium dividing is an example. In sexual reproduction, two gametes join. A mule cannot reproduce but is still alive, because reproduction is needed for the species to continue, not the individual.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='canlilarin-ozellikleri-4' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><line x1='160' y1='20' x2='160' y2='190' stroke='var(--line)'/><text x='80' y='30' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Asexual</text><text x='240' y='30' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Sexual</text><ellipse cx='80' cy='70' rx='24' ry='16' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='80' y1='92' x2='80' y2='114' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#canlilarin-ozellikleri-4)'/><ellipse cx='58' cy='140' rx='18' ry='13' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><ellipse cx='102' cy='140' rx='18' ry='13' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='80' y='182' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>a bacterium divides</text><circle cx='215' cy='72' r='18' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='268' cy='72' r='5' fill='var(--c1)'/><path d='M273,72 q6,-6 12,0 t12,0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='215' y='105' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>egg</text><text x='275' y='105' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>sperm</text><line x1='240' y1='112' x2='240' y2='124' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#canlilarin-ozellikleri-4)'/><circle cx='240' cy='145' r='18' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='240' y='182' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>zygote: two gametes join</text></svg>
cards.key: Asexual reproduction is fast, and the offspring resemble the parent. Sexual reproduction gives high variety.

once.soru: A bacterium reproduces by dividing in two. How do the offspring compare with the parent?

secenekler.neden: The parent copies its genetic material and divides, so the offspring are like copies of the parent. This is called asexual reproduction.
Variety increases when the gametes of two parents join. Division makes copies.
In division, both offspring get the same genetic material.

cards.p: Growth is an increase in mass as the number or size of cells increases. Development is the maturing of structures and functions. A seed becoming a seedling and a caterpillar becoming a butterfly are examples of development.

cards.key: Growth is an increase in amount. Development is maturing and gaining new abilities.

once.soru: A salt crystal and a seedling both grow. What makes the seedling's growth different?

secenekler.neden: The seedling processes nutrients in its cells and makes new cells. A crystal grows by adding matter to its surface and has no metabolism.
Speed is not the difference. Some crystals grow faster than seedlings.
A crystal also gets bigger. The difference is in how the growth happens.

cards.p: Living things sense stimuli such as light, heat and touch, and respond to them. Pulling your hand away from a hot stove and a sensitive plant folding its leaves are examples. The response is often a movement.

cards.p: Even when outside conditions change, a living thing keeps inner conditions such as body temperature, blood sugar and water content within narrow limits. This is called homeostasis. Sweating in the heat and shivering in the cold are examples.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='40' y='80' width='260' height='40' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.2'/><line x1='40' y1='30' x2='40' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)'/><line x1='40' y1='170' x2='305' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)'/><line x1='40' y1='100' x2='300' y2='100' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='4 4'/><path d='M40,100 C70,70 90,70 110,100 S150,130 180,100 S220,70 250,100 S290,130 300,110' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='36' y='104' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end'>37°C</text><text x='75' y='62' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>sweating</text><text x='145' y='142' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>shivering</text><text x='44' y='24' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>body temperature</text><text x='300' y='188' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>time</text><text x='44' y='188' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>green band: normal range</text></svg>
cards.key: Homeostasis is keeping the inner environment steady while the outside world changes.

cards.p: An adaptation is an inherited trait that raises an organism's chance of surviving and reproducing. Adaptations build up over generations through natural selection. The change over time in populations, groups of the same species living together, is called evolution.

once.soru: A cactus's leaves have turned into spines. How does this help in the desert?

secenekler.neden: With less leaf surface, less water is lost by transpiration. Spines also protect the plant from animals. Inherited fits like this are called adaptations.
In a cactus, the green stem does the photosynthesis. Spines do not increase it.
Cacti grow slowly. The main job of the spines is to save water.

cards.p: Viruses are not cells. They are made of a protein coat with DNA or RNA inside it. They can multiply only inside a living cell, so they are considered to be between living and nonliving.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><polygon points='65,55 100,75 100,115 65,135 30,115 30,75' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M45,95 q5,-12 10,0 t10,0 t10,0 t10,0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='65' y='155' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>protein coat</text><text x='65' y='172' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>+ DNA or RNA</text><text x='140' y='35' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)'>Like living things:</text><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='148' y='53'>• has genetic material</text><text x='148' y='69'>• multiplies inside cells</text><text x='148' y='85'>• mutates</text></g><text x='140' y='115' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)'>Like nonliving things:</text><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='148' y='133'>• no cell structure</text><text x='148' y='149'>• no metabolism</text><text x='148' y='165'>• can be crystallized</text></g></svg>
cards.key: Outside a cell, a virus acts like a nonliving thing. Inside a cell, it acts like a living thing.

cards.h: The scientific method: setting up an experiment
cards.p: A biologist first forms a hypothesis and tests it with an experiment. Only one factor is changed in the experiment. This is called the independent variable. The measured result is called the dependent variable. A control group makes comparison possible.

cards.key: A theory is a broad explanation, and a law describes a relationship. So a theory does not turn into a law over time.

once.soru: You are testing how fertilizer affects plant height, and you gave one pot fertilizer. What do you do with the second pot?

secenekler.neden: If everything is kept the same and only the fertilizer differs, the fertilizer causes any difference in height. The pot without fertilizer is the control group.
Then you can't compare with the no-fertilizer case, and you can't see the fertilizer's effect.
If the plant species also changes, you can't know what caused the difference. Only one factor should change in an experiment.

cards.p: Some discoveries changed our lives completely. The cell was first seen in 1665, and the first vaccine was made in 1796. In the 1860s, people learned that germs cause disease. Penicillin was found in 1928, the structure of DNA was solved in 1953, and the human genome was read in 2003.

cards.key: Vaccines and antibiotics deserve the most credit for longer average life spans.

once.soru: Over the last 150 years, the average human life span has more than doubled. What deserves the most credit?

secenekler.neden: In the past, many children died of infections. Vaccines and antibiotics largely prevented this. Clean water and hygiene also helped.
The telescope changed astronomy, but it had no direct effect on health.
This invention changed industry. Discoveries in medicine are what lengthened life spans.

cards.p: Scientific research must also follow ethical rules. Informed consent is obtained from volunteers who take part in studies, and animal experiments need approval from an ethics committee. Making up data, altering data and passing off someone else's work as your own (plagiarism) are fraud.

once.soru: A researcher deletes two measurements from a table because they didn't give the expected result. What is this?

secenekler.neden: Deleting an unwanted result is altering the data. Whatever the result, it must be reported as it is.
Data cannot be deleted unless a measurement error is proven, because deleting it distorts the result.
Data cannot be picked to suit the researcher. It must be reported as it is.

cards.p:
• Living things are made of cells and form a layered order.
• They feed, carry out respiration and excretion, and use energy through ATP.
• They reproduce, grow, develop and respond to stimuli.
• They keep their inner balance through homeostasis. Populations adapt to their environment over generations.
• Science advances through hypotheses and controlled experiments.

quiz.q: A student is studying how music affects the number of fruits on tomato plants. Match each term with what it means in this experiment.
ciftler: Plants in the greenhouse with no music
quiz.e: The only factor changed in the experiment is music, and the measured result is the number of fruits. Everything except music is kept the same, and the greenhouse with no music is the control group.

quiz.q: Put each process in the right branch of metabolism.
quiz.e: Building large molecules from small ones is anabolism, and it uses energy. Making protein, glycogen, and glucose in photosynthesis are examples. Breaking down large molecules is catabolism. Digestion, respiration and the breakdown of fats are examples.

quiz.q: Match each example with the trait of life it shows.
quiz.e: Keeping the inner environment steady is homeostasis. Thick fur that makes survival easier is an inherited adaptation. The maturing of structures is development, offspring from a single parent is asexual reproduction, and bending toward light is a response to stimuli.

quiz.q: A muscle cell holds very little ATP at any moment, but a muscle can work for hours. Why?
o: ATP is constantly remade from ADP and phosphate
Muscle uses energy directly from glucose
ATP rejoins by itself after it splits
Muscle takes ready-made ATP from the blood
quiz.e: The energy released in respiration recharges ATP by adding phosphate to ADP. This cycle never stops.
y: A cell cannot use the energy in food directly. It must first pass this energy to ATP.
Adding phosphate to ADP takes energy, and that energy comes from respiration.
ATP is not carried between cells. Each cell makes its own ATP.

biyomolekuller.title: Biomolecules
biyomolekuller.summary: Which molecules are living things made of, and what do they do?

cards.p: Water makes up about 70% of a cell's mass. It dissolves substances and keeps body temperature steady. Minerals give no energy but regulate processes in the body. Water and minerals are inorganic substances. The other biomolecules, which have a carbon skeleton, are organic.

cards.key: Water, minerals and vitamins are absorbed without being digested. A living thing takes in water and minerals ready-made from outside.

once.soru: When you sweat, you lose water and salt (minerals). Do minerals give the body energy?

secenekler.neden: Minerals give no energy. They play a regulating role. For example, calcium is needed for bones, iron for hemoglobin, and sodium and potassium for nerve signals.
Energy comes from carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Minerals are regulators.
Minerals give no energy at all. Their job is to regulate processes in the body.

cards.h: Water leaves as units join, and enters as they split
cards.p: Small units (monomers) join to form large molecules (polymers). Water is released as they join, and this is called dehydration synthesis. In the reverse, water is added and the bond breaks. This is called hydrolysis. Digestion is hydrolysis.

cards.key: In dehydration, units join and water is released. In hydrolysis, water is added and the bond breaks.

cards.p: Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and they are a living thing's first choice of energy source. Glucose, fructose, galactose, ribose and deoxyribose are monosaccharides. When two monosaccharides join, a disaccharide forms: maltose, sucrose and lactose.

once.soru: Table sugar (sucrose) forms when two small sugars join. What is released as they join?

secenekler.neden: One water molecule is released in each join: glucose + fructose → sucrose + water. When two monosaccharides join, a disaccharide forms.
CO₂ is released when sugars are burned in respiration, not when they join.
The molecule that leaves during the join is water, not oxygen.

cards.p: Many glucose molecules join to form polysaccharides. Starch is the storage form in plants, and glycogen in animals. Cellulose makes up plant cell walls, and humans cannot digest it. Chitin is a polysaccharide that makes up the exoskeleton of insects.

cards.key: Glycogen is highly branched. So glucose can be cut from many ends at once, and energy is supplied fast.

cards.p: Lipids do not dissolve in water. A fat molecule (triglyceride) is made of 1 glycerol and 3 fatty acids. A gram of fat gives more than twice the energy of a gram of carbohydrate. That is why fat is used for long-term storage, and it also insulates the body against cold.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='24' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids = triglyceride</text><rect x='40' y='45' width='40' height='110' rx='6' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2'/><g fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' stroke-linejoin='round'><polyline points='80,62 95,54 110,62 125,54 140,62 155,54 170,62 185,54 200,62 215,54 230,62'/><polyline points='80,100 95,92 110,100 125,92 140,100 155,92 170,100 185,92 200,100 215,92 230,100'/><polyline points='80,138 95,130 110,138 125,130 140,138 155,130 170,138 185,130 200,138 215,130 230,138'/></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='238' y='62'>fatty acid</text><text x='238' y='100'>fatty acid</text><text x='238' y='138'>fatty acid</text></g><text x='60' y='178' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>glycerol</text><text x='300' y='178' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>≈9 kcal/g (carbohydrate ≈4)</text></svg>
cards.key: Breaking down fat also releases more metabolic water than carbohydrate does. Camels and hibernating animals use this water.

cards.p: In saturated fatty acids, there are only single bonds between the carbons. Their chains are straight, so they pack tightly. That is why butter is solid. In unsaturated fatty acids, a double bond bends the chain. Bent chains cannot pack tightly. That is why olive oil is liquid.

cards.key: Omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids are essential. The body cannot make them, so we must get them from food.

once.soru: Butter is solid at room temperature, and olive oil is liquid. What causes the difference?

secenekler.yazi: The shape of the fatty acids
secenekler.neden: The saturated fatty acids in butter have straight chains that pack tightly. In olive oil, a double bond bends the chain, so they cannot pack tightly.
Color does not decide a fat's melting point.
Even at the same mass, one is solid and the other is liquid. The difference is in the shape of the molecules.

cards.p: A phospholipid has a water-loving head and two water-avoiding tails. Phospholipids line up in a double layer to form the cell membrane. Steroids are molecules with four rings. Cholesterol, estrogen, testosterone and vitamin D are steroids.

cards.key: Phospholipids form the framework of the cell membrane. Cholesterol keeps the fluidity of animal cell membranes steady.

once.soru: The molecule that builds the cell membrane has one water-loving end and one water-avoiding end. There is water both inside and outside the cell. How do these molecules line up?

secenekler.neden: The water-loving heads face the water on both sides. The water-avoiding tails turn toward each other in the middle, forming a phospholipid double layer.
The tails avoid water, so they do not face it.
The molecules do not spread randomly. The water-loving and water-avoiding ends form an orderly double layer.

cards.p: Proteins do many jobs in the body. As enzymes they speed up reactions, like keratin they form structures, and like hemoglobin they transport things. They act in defense as antibodies, as hormones such as insulin, and they make movement possible. If heat or extreme pH damages the shape (denaturation), the protein cannot do its job.

once.soru: When an egg is cooked, the white turns opaque and firm and never goes back. What happened to the protein in the egg white?

secenekler.neden: Heat damaged the protein's folded shape. This is called denaturation. A protein that has lost its shape cannot do its job.
Egg white is still protein. Only its shape changed.
Drying does not turn egg white opaque. Heat changed the protein's structure.

cards.p: The unit of nucleic acids is the nucleotide. It is made of a phosphate, a sugar and a base. DNA is double-stranded, carries the sugar deoxyribose and the bases A, T, G and C, and stores information. RNA is usually single-stranded, carries ribose, has U instead of T, and uses the information.

cards.p: Vitamins give no energy and are needed in small amounts. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in the body. Most water-soluble vitamins (B, C) are not stored, and any extra leaves in urine.

cards.key: The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K.

etk.soru: Put each vitamin in the right group: does it dissolve in fat or in water?
ogeler: Vitamin D dissolves in fat and can be stored in the body.
Vitamin C dissolves in water. Any extra leaves in urine, so it must be taken regularly.
B<sub>12</sub> dissolves in water. Even so, it can be stored in the liver for years.

once.soru: For someone who takes too many vitamin pills, which is riskier?

secenekler.neden: Vitamin A dissolves in fat and builds up in the body. Too much can cause poisoning.
Vitamin C dissolves in water, and any extra leaves in urine.
The difference is in what they dissolve in: fat-soluble ones build up, and water-soluble ones are flushed out.

cards.key: Sucrose is not a reducing sugar, so it does not change the color of Benedict's solution.

once.soru: When iodine was dropped on a potato slice, it turned blue-black. What is in the potato?

secenekler.neden: Iodine turns blue-black with starch. A potato is the plant's starch store.
Biuret shows protein by turning purple. Iodine does not show protein.
Sudan III stains fat red. Iodine does not show fat.

cards.p:
• Water dissolves substances, and minerals regulate processes in the body.
• Carbohydrates give quick energy, fats are long-term storage, and phospholipids build membranes.
• Proteins form structures and do work: enzymes, transport, defense.
• Nucleic acids carry genetic information, and vitamins are regulators.
• Large molecules are built by dehydration and broken down by hydrolysis.

quiz.q: Put each molecule in its biomolecule group.
quiz.e: Starch, cellulose and lactose are carbohydrates made of sugars. Cholesterol and testosterone are steroids, and phospholipid is the lipid of membranes. Keratin and antibodies are proteins made of amino acid chains.

quiz.q: Match each mineral with its job in the body.
quiz.e: Calcium is found in bones and teeth, iron in hemoglobin, and iodine in thyroid hormone. Sodium and potassium are needed for nerve signals. Minerals give no energy. They are regulators.

quiz.q: 3 separate straight-chain peptides are made, each of 10 amino acids. How many water molecules are released in total?
quiz.e: Each chain forms 10 − 1 = 9 peptide bonds, and one water is released per bond. Across three separate chains, 3 × 9 = 27 waters are released.

quiz.q: Sort each structure by where it is found.
quiz.e: Deoxyribose and thymine are found only in DNA, and ribose and uracil only in RNA. Phosphate and the bases adenine, guanine and cytosine are found in both.

enzimler.title: Enzymes
enzimler.summary: How do the molecules that speed up reactions in the cell work?

cards.p: Enzymes are molecules, mostly proteins, that speed up reactions in the cell. They lower the activation energy needed for a reaction to start. But they do not change the product or the overall energy difference of the reaction.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><line x1='35' y1='25' x2='35' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)'/><line x1='35' y1='170' x2='300' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)'/><path d='M45,110 L90,110 C120,110 130,40 160,40 C190,40 200,150 230,150 L295,150' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M45,110 L90,110 C120,110 130,85 160,85 C190,85 200,150 230,150 L295,150' fill='none' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2.5' stroke-dasharray='6 4'/><text x='112' y='40' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end'>without enzyme</text><text x='160' y='102' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle'>with enzyme</text><text x='45' y='104' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>substrate</text><text x='262' y='144' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>product</text><text x='40' y='20' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>energy</text><text x='300' y='188' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>reaction progress</text></svg>
cards.key: An enzyme is a biological catalyst that lowers activation energy.

cards.p: The substance an enzyme acts on is called the substrate. The substrate binds to the enzyme's active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex. After the products leave, the enzyme stays unchanged and is used again.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='enzimler-2' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><g fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'><path d='M10,100 L30,100 L30,112 L50,112 L50,100 L70,100 L70,140 Q40,155 10,140 Z'/><path d='M120,100 L140,100 L140,112 L160,112 L160,100 L180,100 L180,140 Q150,155 120,140 Z'/><path d='M230,100 L250,100 L250,112 L270,112 L270,100 L290,100 L290,140 Q260,155 230,140 Z'/></g><g fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2'><rect x='15' y='45' width='20' height='24'/><rect x='140' y='88' width='20' height='24'/><rect x='245' y='62' width='10' height='22'/><rect x='268' y='58' width='10' height='22'/></g><text x='75' y='70' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>active site</text><line x1='73' y1='72' x2='45' y2='104' stroke='var(--muted)'/><g stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#enzimler-2)'><line x1='78' y1='125' x2='112' y2='125'/><line x1='188' y1='125' x2='222' y2='125'/></g><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='40' y='175'>E + S</text><text x='150' y='175'>ES complex</text><text x='260' y='175'>E + products</text></g><text x='260' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>enzyme stays the same</text></svg>
cards.key: The enzyme and substrate join, the product forms, and the enzyme is set free: E + S → ES → E + product.

cards.h: Lock and key, or induced fit?
cards.p: According to the lock-and-key model, the active site fits the substrate exactly from the start. According to the induced fit model, which is accepted today, the active site is flexible. It wraps around the substrate the way a glove fits a hand.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 210'><defs><marker id='enzimler-3' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='10' y='20' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)'>Lock and key</text><g fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'><path d='M40,50 L70,50 L80,65 L90,50 L120,50 L120,85 L40,85 Z'/><path d='M190,50 L220,50 L230,65 L240,50 L270,50 L270,85 L190,85 Z'/></g><g fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.6' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2'><polygon points='70,28 90,28 80,43'/><polygon points='220,50 240,50 230,65'/></g><line x1='135' y1='65' x2='172' y2='65' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#enzimler-3)'/><text x='230' y='102' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>fits exactly beforehand</text><text x='10' y='124' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)'>Induced fit</text><g fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'><path d='M40,150 L65,150 Q80,170 95,150 L120,150 L120,185 L40,185 Z'/><path d='M190,150 L214,150 L219,137 C219,160 241,160 241,137 L246,150 L270,150 L270,185 L190,185 Z'/></g><g fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.6' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2'><circle cx='80' cy='134' r='9'/><circle cx='230' cy='146' r='9'/></g><line x1='135' y1='165' x2='172' y2='165' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#enzimler-3)'/><text x='230' y='202' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>enzyme changes shape to wrap</text></svg>
cards.key: According to the induced fit model, the active site is flexible and takes shape around the substrate.

once.soru: Scientists saw an enzyme's active site change shape slightly as the substrate bound. What is the active site like?

secenekler.neden: The active site is flexible, and when the substrate binds, it wraps around it like a glove. This is called induced fit.
If the active site were rigid, it could not change shape. The old lock-and-key model thought so.
The active site has a specific shape. Without one, it would bind to any substance.

cards.p: Each enzyme usually acts only on a particular substrate. This is called specificity. Most enzyme names are made by adding -ase to the name of the substrate. For example, the enzyme that breaks down lactose is called lactase.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='enzimler-4' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><path d='M110,110 L145,110 L145,128 L175,128 L175,110 L210,110 L210,150 L110,150 Z' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='160' y='143' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>enzyme</text><rect x='40' y='60' width='30' height='18' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='240,78 270,78 255,55' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='72' y1='80' x2='140' y2='115' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#enzimler-4)'/><line x1='245' y1='85' x2='205' y2='105' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><path d='M45,40 L52,48 L66,32' fill='none' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='3'/><g stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3'><line x1='276' y1='34' x2='290' y2='48'/><line x1='290' y1='34' x2='276' y2='48'/></g><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'><text x='55' y='100' fill='var(--c3)'>fits</text><text x='270' y='105' fill='var(--c2)'>doesn't fit</text></g><text x='160' y='182' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>lactase breaks down only lactose</text></svg>
cards.key: Lactase breaks down lactose, maltase breaks down maltose, and lipase breaks down lipids.

cards.p: An enzyme works fastest at its optimum temperature. In humans, this is about 37 °C. If the temperature rises too much, the enzyme's shape is damaged. This is called denaturation, and it is usually permanent. Cold does not damage an enzyme, it only slows it down.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><line x1='40' y1='25' x2='40' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)'/><line x1='40' y1='170' x2='305' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)'/><path d='M40,162 C90,155 140,120 165,55 C170,43 178,43 185,60 L220,166' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'/><line x1='172' y1='48' x2='172' y2='170' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='172' y='36' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>optimum ≈37 °C</text><text x='225' y='100' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)'>denaturation</text><text x='80' y='135' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>slow in the cold</text><g font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='40' y='186'>0</text><text x='172' y='186'>37</text><text x='254' y='186'>60</text></g><text x='44' y='20' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>reaction rate</text><text x='232' y='158' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>temperature °C</text></svg>
cards.key: Cold slows an enzyme, and this effect is reversible. Too much heat damages the enzyme, usually permanently.

cards.p: Each enzyme has a pH at which it works best. Pepsin in the stomach works fastest at about pH 2, and trypsin in the intestine at about pH 8. A very acidic or basic environment damages the enzyme's shape.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><line x1='40' y1='25' x2='40' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)'/><line x1='40' y1='170' x2='305' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)'/><path d='M40,165 C60,160 65,50 77,50 C89,50 95,160 115,165' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M150,165 C170,160 177,50 189,50 C201,50 208,160 228,165' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='77' y='40' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>pepsin (stomach)</text><text x='189' y='40' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>trypsin (small intestine)</text><g font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='40' y='186'>0</text><text x='77' y='186'>2</text><text x='189' y='186'>8</text><text x='296' y='186'>14</text></g><text x='300' y='155' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>pH</text><text x='44' y='20' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>rate</text></svg>
cards.key: Pepsin works well in an acidic environment, and trypsin in a slightly basic one.

cards.p: When the amount of enzyme is fixed, the reaction rate rises as substrate increases. Once all active sites are full, the rate rises no further. This is called saturation. Adding enzyme raises the rate. If substrate is fixed, the amount of product does not change, it only forms faster.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 205'><g stroke='var(--ink)'><line x1='25' y1='40' x2='25' y2='160'/><line x1='25' y1='160' x2='150' y2='160'/><line x1='180' y1='40' x2='180' y2='160'/><line x1='180' y1='160' x2='305' y2='160'/></g><line x1='25' y1='58' x2='150' y2='58' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><path d='M25,160 C55,80 90,62 150,60' fill='none' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2.5'/><line x1='180' y1='160' x2='300' y2='50' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='100' y='50' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>saturation</text><g font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'><text x='28' y='32'>rate</text><text x='183' y='32'>rate</text></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='88' y='180'>amount of substrate</text><text x='243' y='180'>amount of enzyme</text></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='88' y='196'>(enzyme fixed)</text><text x='243' y='196'>(plenty of substrate)</text></g></svg>
cards.key: At saturation, what limits the rate is the number of enzymes, not the substrate.

cards.p: Some enzymes work with a helper. The protein part of the enzyme is called the apoenzyme, and the helper is called a cofactor. A cofactor can be an ion such as Mg²⁺ or Zn²⁺. Organic cofactors are called coenzymes, and most are made from B vitamins.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='enzimler-8' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><path d='M20,70 L45,70 L45,85 L60,85 L60,70 L85,70 L85,110 Q52,125 20,110 Z' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='103' y='98' font-size='15' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>+</text><circle cx='125' cy='92' r='10' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.6' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='145' y1='92' x2='205' y2='92' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#enzimler-8)'/><path d='M215,70 L240,70 L240,85 L255,85 L255,70 L280,70 L280,110 Q247,125 215,110 Z' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='247.5' cy='78' r='7' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.6' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2'/><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='52' y='140'>Apoenzyme</text><text x='125' y='140'>Cofactor</text><text x='247' y='140'>Holoenzyme</text></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='52' y='56'>protein</text><text x='247' y='56'>working enzyme</text></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='20' y='170'>Inorganic cofactors: Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺</text><text x='20' y='190'>Organic ones = coenzymes (B vitamins)</text></g></svg>
cards.key: When the apoenzyme and cofactor join, the working enzyme, the holoenzyme, forms.

once.soru: Some enzymes do not work without a small helper. Where do these helpers mostly come from?

secenekler.neden: Minerals such as Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ and coenzymes made from B vitamins help enzymes. This is one reason we need vitamins, even in small amounts.
Fats are energy stores. They do not help enzymes.
Cellulose makes up plant cell walls. Humans can't even digest it.

cards.p: A substance that slows an enzyme down is called an inhibitor. A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and blocks the active site. A noncompetitive inhibitor binds to another part of the enzyme and changes the enzyme's shape.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 205'><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='60' y='30'>Competitive</text><text x='230' y='30'>Noncompetitive</text></g><line x1='150' y1='20' x2='150' y2='200' stroke='var(--line)'/><path d='M20,110 L50,110 L50,125 L70,125 L70,110 L100,110 L100,150 Q60,165 20,150 Z' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='50' y='103' width='20' height='22' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='60' y='119' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>I</text><rect x='75' y='60' width='20' height='22' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='85' y='76' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>S</text><g stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'><line x1='102' y1='62' x2='112' y2='72'/><line x1='112' y1='62' x2='102' y2='72'/></g><path d='M180,110 L210,110 L215,122 L225,118 L235,110 L265,110 L265,150 Q222,165 180,150 Z' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='272' cy='132' r='9' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='272' y='136' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>I</text><rect x='212' y='60' width='20' height='22' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='222' y='76' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>S</text><g stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'><line x1='238' y1='62' x2='248' y2='72'/><line x1='248' y1='62' x2='238' y2='72'/></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='70' y='182'>blocks the active site</text><text x='230' y='182'>binds elsewhere</text></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='70' y='198'>resembles the substrate</text><text x='230' y='198'>active site is distorted</text></g></svg>
cards.key: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site. A noncompetitive inhibitor changes the enzyme's shape.

etk.soru: Which inhibitor does each feature belong to?
ogeler: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the same spot. With more substrate, it blocks the active site less often.
More substrate doesn't remove its effect
A noncompetitive inhibitor binds somewhere else. Even with more substrate, the misshapen enzyme does not work.

cards.p: A substance that speeds up an enzyme is called an activator. For example, the Cl⁻ ion activates salivary amylase, which digests starch. Stomach acid also activates pepsin. In reversible reactions, an enzyme speeds up both directions but does not change the ratio at equilibrium.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='enzimler-akt' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='78' y='24'>Activator</text><text x='240' y='24'>Reversible reaction</text></g><line x1='160' y1='12' x2='160' y2='196' stroke='var(--line)'/><path d='M30,60 L55,60 L55,75 L70,75 L70,60 L95,60 L95,100 Q62,115 30,100 Z' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='112' cy='92' r='12' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.4' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='112' y='96' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Cl⁻</text><rect x='52' y='38' width='21' height='16' rx='3' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.6' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2'/><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'><text x='78' y='134' fill='var(--ink)'>amylase + Cl⁻</text><text x='78' y='150' fill='var(--muted)'>works faster</text><text x='78' y='176' fill='var(--ink)'>pepsinogen → pepsin</text><text x='78' y='192' fill='var(--muted)'>(by stomach acid)</text></g><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='240' y='60'>CO₂ + H₂O</text><text x='240' y='126'>H₂CO₃</text></g><g stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#enzimler-akt)'><line x1='228' y1='70' x2='228' y2='108'/><line x1='252' y1='108' x2='252' y2='70'/></g><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'><text x='240' y='150' fill='var(--c5)'>carbonic anhydrase</text><text x='240' y='168' fill='var(--muted)'>speeds up both directions</text><text x='240' y='186' fill='var(--muted)'>doesn't change the equilibrium</text></g></svg>
cards.key: An activator speeds an enzyme up, and an inhibitor slows it down.

once.soru: The stomach first releases pepsin as inactive pepsinogen. What turns it into working pepsin?

secenekler.neden: Stomach acid (HCl) turns pepsinogen into pepsin. Releasing pepsin in an inactive form protects the stomach wall.
Saliva works in the mouth, not the stomach, and it contains amylase.
Bile breaks fats into small droplets in the small intestine.

cards.p: Enzymes also work outside cells when they find the right temperature and pH. Digestive enzymes work in the intestine, and enzymes in detergent work on laundry. Enzyme reactions need water to take place.

cards.key: An enzyme needs the right environment and water to work, not a living cell.

once.soru: In a dry seed, enzymes barely work. What does the seed need to take in for them to start working?

secenekler.neden: Enzyme reactions take place in water. When the seed takes in water, the enzymes work and the seed germinates.
Germination also starts underground, in the dark. What is really needed is water.
CO₂ is needed for photosynthesis. What starts germination is water.

cards.p:
• Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering activation energy and are used again.
• The substrate binds specifically to the active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
• Temperature, pH and the amounts of substrate and enzyme affect the rate. Too much heat and the wrong pH damage the enzyme.
• Cofactors and activators help enzymes, and inhibitors block them.

quiz.q: Put an enzyme's working cycle in order.
ogeler: Substrate binds to the active site
The unchanged enzyme binds a new substrate
quiz.e: When the substrate binds to the active site, an enzyme-substrate complex forms. Then the reaction takes place and the products leave. The enzyme is not used up in the reaction, so it is used again and again.

quiz.q: When a suitable enzyme is added to a reaction, what changes and what doesn't? Sort them.
quiz.e: An enzyme lowers the activation energy. So the reaction speeds up and equilibrium is reached sooner. It does not change the type of product, the total amount of product, the energy difference or the ratios at equilibrium.

quiz.q: Match each term with its correct definition.
ciftler: The protein part of an enzyme
Binds elsewhere and changes the shape
quiz.e: The apoenzyme is the protein part of an enzyme, and a coenzyme is an organic cofactor, mostly made from B vitamins. An activator speeds the enzyme up. A competitive inhibitor blocks the active site, and a noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the shape.

quiz.q: In two separate tubes, pepsin and trypsin work on their own substrates at 37 °C. If the pH of both tubes is raised from 2 to 8, how do the reaction rates change?
o: Pepsin slows down, trypsin speeds up
Both speed up
Pepsin speeds up, trypsin slows down
Neither changes
quiz.e: Pepsin works best at about pH 2, and trypsin at about pH 8. As the pH rises toward 8, pepsin moves away from its best value and trypsin moves closer.
y: Each enzyme has its own suitable pH. Pepsin likes an acidic environment and slows down in a basic one.
You have it backward. Pepsin is fastest in stomach acid (pH ≈ 2), and trypsin in the slightly basic small intestine (pH ≈ 8).
pH affects the shape of the active site. So even with a fixed temperature, the rate changes with pH.

hucre-organeller.title: Cells and organelles
hucre-organeller.summary: Who does what inside a cell, and how do they work together?

cards.p: According to cell theory, all living things are made of cells, and the cell is the unit of structure and function in living things. Every cell comes from a cell that already existed. Robert Hooke first gave the cell its name in 1665.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><g fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'><rect x='22' y='32' width='14' height='14'/><rect x='36' y='32' width='14' height='14'/><rect x='22' y='46' width='14' height='14'/><rect x='36' y='46' width='14' height='14'/></g><circle cx='36' cy='100' r='15' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='36' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--c1)'/><circle cx='26' cy='155' r='11' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='48' cy='155' r='11' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='75' y='51'>1. All living things are made of cells</text><text x='75' y='105'>2. Cell: unit of structure and function</text><text x='75' y='160'>3. Cells come from cells</text></g><text x='160' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Hooke 1665 · Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow</text></svg>
cards.key: Every cell comes from a cell that already existed.

once.soru: Where does a new cell come from?

secenekler.neden: Every cell forms when an existing cell divides. This is one of the basic principles of cell theory.
Pasteur's experiments showed that life does not arise on its own from nonliving matter.
Food gives the cell building blocks and energy. But a new cell forms by division.

cards.p: Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, have no membrane-bound nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Their DNA floats free in the cytoplasm. In eukaryotes, such as plants, animals and fungi, the DNA is inside a nucleus. The cell membrane, ribosomes and DNA are found in both cell types.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='80' y='30' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Prokaryote</text><text x='240' y='30' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Eukaryote</text><rect x='20' y='60' width='110' height='60' rx='30' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M130,90 q8,-10 16,0 t14,0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M50,90 q6,-14 14,-2 t14,4 t12,-6 t10,8' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><g fill='var(--ink)'><circle cx='40' cy='75' r='2'/><circle cx='60' cy='108' r='2'/><circle cx='95' cy='72' r='2'/><circle cx='110' cy='104' r='2'/><circle cx='80' cy='110' r='2'/></g><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'><text x='80' y='145' fill='var(--ink)'>no nucleus</text><text x='80' y='162' fill='var(--muted)'>DNA in cytoplasm</text></g><circle cx='240' cy='95' r='55' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='240' cy='95' r='18' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M232,95 q4,-6 8,0 t8,0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><ellipse cx='210' cy='125' rx='12' ry='6' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c2)'/><path d='M262,65 q8,6 16,0 M262,73 q8,6 16,0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2'/><g fill='var(--ink)'><circle cx='270' cy='120' r='2'/><circle cx='215' cy='70' r='2'/><circle cx='250' cy='130' r='2'/></g><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'><text x='240' y='168' fill='var(--ink)'>membrane-bound nucleus</text><text x='240' y='185' fill='var(--muted)'>membrane-bound organelles</text></g></svg>
cards.key: Prokaryote means "before the nucleus", and eukaryote means "with a true nucleus".

cards.p: The cell membrane surrounds the cell and chooses which substances go in and out. That is why the membrane is called selectively permeable. The jelly-like fluid that fills the cell is called cytoplasm. Organelles and many reactions are found in the cytoplasm.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='hucre-organeller-3' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='22' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Membrane: selectively permeable boundary</text><ellipse cx='140' cy='105' rx='110' ry='70' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.1' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='140' cy='95' r='20' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><ellipse cx='88' cy='78' rx='14' ry='7' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c2)'/><ellipse cx='195' cy='125' rx='14' ry='7' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c2)'/><g fill='var(--ink)'><circle cx='180' cy='70' r='2'/><circle cx='70' cy='120' r='2'/><circle cx='165' cy='150' r='2'/><circle cx='210' cy='90' r='2'/></g><text x='100' y='145' font-size='13' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>cytoplasm</text><line x1='4' y1='100' x2='38' y2='100' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#hucre-organeller-3)'/><line x1='42' y1='118' x2='8' y2='118' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#hucre-organeller-3)'/><text x='262' y='60' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)'>membrane</text><line x1='258' y1='57' x2='226' y2='62' stroke='var(--muted)'/><text x='258' y='190' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>controls entry and exit</text></svg>

once.soru: What does the membrane around a cell do?

secenekler.yazi: Chooses what goes in and out
secenekler.neden: The membrane is selectively permeable. It takes in what is needed, sends out wastes and keeps harmful substances outside.
If the membrane let everything through, it couldn't protect the inside of the cell.
If the membrane let nothing through, the cell couldn't take in food or get rid of wastes.

cards.p: The nucleus is surrounded by a double membrane with pores. Inside are DNA and the nucleolus, which helps make ribosomes. DNA decides which proteins are made. That is why the nucleus is the cell's control center.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='20' y='22' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)'>Nucleus</text><circle cx='120' cy='100' r='62' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='120' cy='100' r='56' fill='none' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><g fill='var(--c4)'><circle cx='120' cy='41' r='4'/><circle cx='179' cy='100' r='4'/><circle cx='120' cy='159' r='4'/><circle cx='61' cy='100' r='4'/><circle cx='162' cy='58' r='4'/></g><path d='M85,90 q10,-15 20,0 t20,0 t20,0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M85,120 q10,-12 20,0 t20,0 t20,0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='140' cy='145' r='10' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c2)'/><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='200' y='40'>pore</text><text x='200' y='85'>double membrane</text><text x='200' y='120'>DNA (chromatin)</text><text x='200' y='160'>nucleolus</text></g><g stroke='var(--muted)'><line x1='196' y1='37' x2='166' y2='55'/><line x1='196' y1='82' x2='181' y2='88'/><line x1='196' y1='117' x2='147' y2='120'/><line x1='196' y1='157' x2='151' y2='148'/></g></svg>
cards.key: The information in DNA is like the cell's instruction book.

once.soru: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus. So what can't they do?

secenekler.neden: Before a cell divides, it must copy its DNA. A red blood cell with no nucleus has no DNA to copy. Red blood cells live about 120 days, and new ones are made in the bone marrow.
A red blood cell carries oxygen with hemoglobin. Having no nucleus makes room for more hemoglobin.
Blood flow carries red blood cells. This has nothing to do with the nucleus.

cards.p: A ribosome is a structure without a membrane, and it makes proteins. Rough ER has ribosomes on its surface. It makes and carries proteins that will be secreted. Smooth ER makes lipids, and in the liver it makes harmful substances harmless.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='80' y='30' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Rough ER</text><text x='240' y='30' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Smooth ER</text><g fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'><rect x='25' y='55' width='110' height='14' rx='7'/><rect x='25' y='90' width='110' height='14' rx='7'/><rect x='25' y='125' width='110' height='14' rx='7'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='5' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-dasharray='0 11'><line x1='32' y1='50' x2='130' y2='50'/><line x1='32' y1='74' x2='130' y2='74'/><line x1='32' y1='85' x2='130' y2='85'/><line x1='32' y1='109' x2='130' y2='109'/><line x1='32' y1='120' x2='130' y2='120'/><line x1='32' y1='144' x2='130' y2='144'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='10' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-opacity='0.5'><path d='M190,60 C220,40 250,80 290,60'/><path d='M185,100 C215,120 255,80 295,105'/><path d='M195,140 C230,125 260,150 290,135'/></g><line x1='160' y1='40' x2='160' y2='160' stroke='var(--line)'/><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'><text x='80' y='170' fill='var(--ink)'>protein production</text><text x='80' y='188' fill='var(--muted)'>dots: ribosomes</text><text x='240' y='170' fill='var(--ink)'>lipids, detoxification</text><text x='240' y='188' fill='var(--muted)'>Ca²⁺ store</text></g></svg>
cards.key: Rough ER is the protein production line. Smooth ER makes lipids and neutralizes harmful substances.

once.soru: A cell makes a lot of protein. Which structure does it have plenty of?

secenekler.neden: Ribosomes make proteins. In cells that secrete, rough ER is highly developed.
A vacuole stores substances. It does not make protein.
The centrosome organizes the spindle fibers during division. It does not make protein.

cards.p: The Golgi apparatus modifies proteins coming from the ER, packages them and sends them where they need to go in vesicles. So it is like the cell's shipping center. A lysosome is a vesicle that buds off the Golgi and is full of enzymes. It breaks down food and worn-out organelles.

cards.key: The Golgi is the cell's shipping center, and the lysosome handles digestion and recycling.

cards.p: Mitochondria make ATP from food by aerobic respiration, and their inner membrane is folded. Chloroplasts in plants use light energy for photosynthesis and make glucose. Both organelles have a double membrane and their own DNA.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='80' y='35' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Mitochondrion</text><text x='240' y='35' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Chloroplast</text><ellipse cx='80' cy='90' rx='60' ry='32' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3'/><polyline points='30,90 45,70 55,108 68,70 80,108 92,70 104,108 116,70 130,90' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' stroke-linejoin='round'/><ellipse cx='240' cy='90' rx='60' ry='32' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='196' y1='90' x2='284' y2='90' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><g fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.6' stroke='var(--c3)'><rect x='205' y='74' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='205' y='81' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='205' y='94' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='205' y='101' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='233' y='74' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='233' y='81' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='233' y='94' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='233' y='101' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='261' y='74' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='261' y='81' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='261' y='94' width='18' height='5'/><rect x='261' y='101' width='18' height='5'/></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='80' y='145'>food + O₂ → ATP</text><text x='240' y='145'>light → glucose</text></g><text x='160' y='182' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>both double-membraned, with their own DNA</text></svg>
cards.key: The chloroplast turns light energy into food, and the mitochondrion passes the energy in food to ATP.

cards.p: A peroxisome uses the enzyme catalase to split harmful H₂O₂ into water and oxygen. Plant cells have three kinds of plastids. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, chromoplasts give color, and leucoplasts store starch.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><circle cx='55' cy='60' r='30' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='55' cy='60' r='9' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.4'/><text x='55' y='110' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>peroxisome</text><text x='55' y='126' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>H₂O₂ → water + O₂</text><ellipse cx='140' cy='60' rx='30' ry='18' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='140' y='110' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>chloroplast</text><text x='140' y='126' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>photosynthesis</text><ellipse cx='210' cy='60' rx='30' ry='18' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='210' y='110' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>chromoplast</text><text x='210' y='126' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>gives color</text><ellipse cx='280' cy='60' rx='30' ry='18' fill='var(--line)' fill-opacity='0.9' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='280' y='110' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>leucoplast</text><text x='280' y='126' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>stores starch</text><path d='M115 152 H305' stroke='var(--line)'/><text x='210' y='170' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>three kinds of plastid (plants)</text><text x='55' y='170' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>plentiful in the liver</text></svg>

once.soru: Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) foams when poured on a wound, because an enzyme in the tissue splits it into water and oxygen. Why does the cell do this?

secenekler.neden: H₂O₂ damages the cell. Catalase in peroxisomes splits it right away into water and oxygen. The released oxygen makes the foam.
The cell gets its energy from food in the mitochondria. The purpose of this reaction is to protect the cell.
Very little water is released. The goal is to destroy the harmful substance.

cards.p: A plant cell has a cell wall made of cellulose, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole. An animal cell has none of these. Instead, an animal cell has a centrosome that organizes division.

cards.key: The membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, ribosomes, ER, Golgi and mitochondria are found in both cells.

etk.soru: Tap the numbers. Which structures are in both cells, and which are in only one?

noktalar.acik: The cell wall is made of cellulose. It supports and protects the plant cell and keeps it from bursting when it takes in water. Animal cells don't have one.
Using chlorophyll, the chloroplast captures light energy and makes glucose by photosynthesis. It is found in plants and algae, not in animal cells.
The central vacuole stores water, nutrients, pigments and wastes. When full of water, it keeps the cell firm. Vacuoles in animal cells are small.
The nucleus holds DNA and runs the cell. Plant and animal cells both have one.
The centrosome organizes the spindle fibers when the cell divides. It is found in animal cells. Plant cells build their spindle without a centrosome.
Mitochondria make ATP by aerobic respiration. They are found in both plant and animal cells.
The cell membrane is a selectively permeable boundary found in every cell. In plants, it lies just inside the cell wall.

cards.p: A food vacuole carries food, and the food is digested when it fuses with a lysosome. In freshwater organisms, the contractile vacuole uses ATP to pump out extra water. The central vacuole in plants stores water and keeps the cell firm.

once.soru: Water keeps seeping into a paramecium living in fresh water. What does it do to keep from bursting?

secenekler.yazi: It pumps out the extra water
secenekler.neden: The contractile vacuole uses ATP to pump out the extra water that seeps in.
If it stored the water, it would swell and burst.
Water would still seep in. The solution is to pump the extra water out.

cards.p: The cytoskeleton gives the cell its shape and moves vesicles around. The centrosome organizes the spindle fibers during division. Cilia and flagella make movement possible. Cilia are short and many, and flagella are long and few.

cards.key: Ribosomes and centrosomes have no membrane. The nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts have a double membrane. The other organelles have a single membrane.

once.soru: A sperm cell swims to reach the egg. Which structure does it use?

secenekler.neden: A sperm swims by whipping its long flagellum.
Animal cells have no cell wall. A cell wall doesn't provide movement either.
A vacuole stores substances. It doesn't provide movement.

cards.p: A protein that will be secreted passes along a production line: ribosome and rough ER, Golgi, vesicle and finally the outside of the cell. The vesicle fuses with the cell membrane and releases the secretion outside. This is called exocytosis. Mitochondria supply the energy needed.

ER</text><text x='160' y='125'>Golgi</text><text x='220' y='125'>Vesicle</text><text x='290' y='125'>Outside</text></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='35' y='142'>information</text><text x='96' y='142'>synthesis</text><text x='160' y='142'>packaging</text><text x='220' y='142'>transport</text><text x='288' y='142'>exocytosis</text></g><ellipse cx='160' cy='175' rx='22' ry='10' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='190' y='180' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>mitochondria: ATP</text></svg>
cards.key: In cells that secrete, rough ER and the Golgi are highly developed.

cards.p:
• The cell is the unit of life. Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound nucleus, and eukaryotes do.
• The nucleus runs the cell. Ribosomes and ER make products, the Golgi packages them, and lysosomes digest.
• Mitochondria make ATP, and chloroplasts make food. Peroxisomes break down H₂O₂.
• Plants have a wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole, and animals have a centrosome.
• The contractile vacuole pumps out extra water.

quiz.q: A salivary gland cell makes and secretes the enzyme amylase. Which organelle plays no direct part in this?
o: Rough ER
Golgi apparatus
Lysosome
Ribosome
quiz.e: Amylase is made on ribosomes and carried through the rough ER to the Golgi. The Golgi packages it and sends it out in a vesicle. The lysosome handles digestion inside the cell and is not part of the secretion line.
y: Ribosomes on the rough ER make and carry the secreted protein. This is the first stop on the line.
The Golgi packages the secreted protein and sends it to the cell membrane in vesicles.
Every protein is made on ribosomes. Amylase is a protein too.

quiz.q: Match each structure with its job.
ciftler: Splits H₂O₂ into water and oxygen
quiz.e: Mitochondria make ATP, and lysosomes digest inside the cell with their digestive enzymes. Peroxisomes break down H₂O₂ with catalase, and smooth ER makes lipids. The contractile vacuole pumps out extra water that enters by osmosis.

quiz.q: Sort each structure by the cell it is found in.
quiz.e: The cellulose wall, chloroplasts and large central vacuole are found only in plant cells. Mitochondria, ribosomes, the Golgi and the cell membrane are found in both.

quiz.q: Sort each structure by the cell type it is found in.
quiz.e: The only membrane structure in prokaryotes is the cell membrane. The nuclear membrane and membrane-bound organelles are unique to eukaryotes. Ribosomes, the cell membrane, DNA and cytoplasm are found in every cell.

madde-gecisi.title: Transport across the cell membrane
madde-gecisi.summary: How do substances get in and out through the membrane, and when is energy needed?

cards.p: The cell membrane is made of a double layer of phospholipids, with proteins and carbohydrates among them. The parts of the membrane can slide sideways. That is why the membrane is fluid. Because different parts sit side by side, it is also a mosaic.

cards.key: Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model in 1972. Animal cell membranes also contain cholesterol.

cards.p: The membrane is selectively permeable. Small, fat-soluble substances pass straight through it. Glucose and ions pass with the help of membrane proteins. Very large substances are carried in vesicles.

cards.key: Small substances like O₂ and CO₂ pass easily. Charged or large substances pass through proteins, and very large ones in vesicles.

cards.p: The spontaneous spreading of a substance from where its concentration is high to where it is low is called diffusion. Diffusion uses no ATP. Once the concentrations are equal, net movement stops.

cards.key: Diffusion speeds up as temperature, concentration difference and surface area increase. It also speeds up as particles get smaller. O₂ passing into the blood in the lungs is an example.

cards.p: Glucose and ions cannot cross the membrane on their own. They still move from high to low, but through channel or carrier proteins. This is called facilitated diffusion, and it uses no ATP.

cards.key: Once all the carriers are busy, the rate of movement stops rising.

cards.p: The movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane is called osmosis. Water moves, on balance, from the side with less solute to the side with more solute. In other words, water flows from where water is plentiful to where it is scarce.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='madde-gecisi-5' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='28' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>selectively permeable membrane</text><rect x='40' y='95' width='120' height='65' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.2'/><rect x='160' y='70' width='120' height='90' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.2'/><path d='M40,40 L40,160 L280,160 L280,40' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='160' y1='36' x2='160' y2='160' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><g fill='var(--c2)'><circle cx='185' cy='90' r='5'/><circle cx='215' cy='105' r='5'/><circle cx='250' cy='92' r='5'/><circle cx='195' cy='135' r='5'/><circle cx='235' cy='140' r='5'/><circle cx='265' cy='120' r='5'/><circle cx='110' cy='140' r='5'/></g><line x1='105' y1='118' x2='215' y2='118' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#madde-gecisi-5)'/><text x='130' y='112' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>water</text><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='100' y='180'>less solute</text><text x='220' y='180'>more solute</text></g><text x='220' y='62' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>level rises</text></svg>
cards.key: Water crosses the membrane in both directions. Osmosis describes the direction of net flow. Most water passes through channels called aquaporins.

cards.p: In a hypotonic environment, water enters the cell. A red blood cell swells and can burst. This is called hemolysis. In an isotonic environment, there is no net water movement. In a hypertonic environment, water leaves the cell and the red blood cell shrinks.
