cards.key: That is why the saline given through an IV is isotonic and contains 0.9% NaCl.

cards.p: A plant cell in a hypotonic environment takes in water and presses against its cell wall. This is called turgor. In a hypertonic environment, it loses water and its membrane pulls away from the wall. This is called plasmolysis. The cell returning to normal in pure water is called deplasmolysis.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='57' y='35'>Hypotonic</text><text x='160' y='35'>Isotonic</text><text x='263' y='35'>Hypertonic</text></g><g fill='none' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='4'><rect x='15' y='50' width='85' height='80'/><rect x='118' y='50' width='85' height='80'/><rect x='221' y='50' width='85' height='80'/></g><rect x='19' y='54' width='77' height='72' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--ink)'/><rect x='27' y='62' width='61' height='56' rx='6' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c1)'/><rect x='123' y='55' width='75' height='70' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--ink)'/><rect x='136' y='68' width='49' height='44' rx='6' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c1)'/><ellipse cx='263' cy='90' rx='26' ry='22' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--ink)'/><ellipse cx='263' cy='90' rx='12' ry='9' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c1)'/><g font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='57' y='148'>water enters</text><text x='160' y='148'>no net movement</text><text x='263' y='148'>water leaves</text></g><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='57' y='166'>turgor</text><text x='160' y='166'>limp</text><text x='263' y='166'>plasmolysis</text></g><text x='160' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>green frame: cell wall · blue: vacuole</text></svg>
cards.key: Plants wilt in salty soil because of plasmolysis.

once.soru: What happens if we put a plant cell in pure water?

secenekler.neden: Water flows in, but there is a strong cell wall outside the membrane. The cell presses against the wall, and the wall's resistance stops more water from entering.
A red blood cell can burst, but a plant cell has a wall outside its membrane.
Pure water is more dilute than the inside of the cell. So water does not leave the cell, it flows in.

cards.p: A solution's power to draw water by osmosis is called osmotic pressure, and it rises with concentration. In a plant cell, the suction force is found by subtracting turgor pressure from osmotic pressure.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><g font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)'><line x1='12' y1='14' x2='26' y2='14' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='3'/><text x='30' y='18'>osmotic pressure</text><line x1='118' y1='14' x2='132' y2='14' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='3'/><text x='136' y='18'>turgor pressure</text><line x1='224' y1='14' x2='238' y2='14' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3'/><text x='242' y='18'>suction force</text></g><g stroke='var(--ink)'><line x1='40' y1='32' x2='40' y2='160'/><line x1='40' y1='160' x2='300' y2='160'/></g><line x1='280' y1='80' x2='280' y2='160' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><line x1='40' y1='50' x2='280' y2='80' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><line x1='40' y1='160' x2='280' y2='80' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2.5'/><line x1='40' y1='50' x2='280' y2='160' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'/><g font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='40' y='176'>plasmolysis</text><text x='280' y='176'>full turgor</text></g><text x='160' y='194' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>as the cell takes in water →</text></svg>
cards.key: As the cell takes in water, turgor rises and suction force falls. At full turgor, the suction force is zero.

once.soru: Which plant cell draws in water more strongly?

secenekler.neden: This cell's inside is concentrated, and the wall does not press on it at all. So its pull for water is highest.
This cell is full of water, and the wall presses back on it. It can't take in more water.
Both the concentration inside the two cells and the pressure from the wall differ.

cards.h: Active transport and the Na-K pump
cards.p: Moving a substance from low to high, that is "uphill", is called active transport. It needs a carrier protein and ATP. For example, the Na⁺-K⁺ pump uses each ATP to push 3 Na⁺ ions out and bring 2 K⁺ ions in.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='madde-gecisi-8' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><rect x='0' y='85' width='320' height='35' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--muted)'/><rect x='138' y='70' width='46' height='65' rx='10' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.4' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='130' x2='150' y2='55' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#madde-gecisi-8)'/><line x1='172' y1='55' x2='172' y2='130' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#madde-gecisi-8)'/><text x='144' y='50' font-size='13' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='end'>3 Na⁺</text><text x='178' y='150' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)'>2 K⁺</text><g fill='var(--c4)'><circle cx='40' cy='62' r='6'/><circle cx='75' cy='52' r='6'/><circle cx='235' cy='58' r='6'/><circle cx='262' cy='68' r='6'/><circle cx='292' cy='52' r='6'/><circle cx='105' cy='66' r='6'/></g><g fill='var(--c3)'><circle cx='40' cy='148' r='6'/><circle cx='72' cy='165' r='6'/><circle cx='232' cy='162' r='6'/><circle cx='272' cy='148' r='6'/><circle cx='298' cy='170' r='6'/></g><text x='108' y='168' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end'>ATP</text><line x1='112' y1='160' x2='136' y2='138' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#madde-gecisi-8)'/><text x='10' y='28' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>outside: more Na⁺</text><text x='10' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>inside: more K⁺</text><text x='310' y='28' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>low to high: uphill</text></svg>
cards.key: Passive transport also happens across the membrane of a dead cell, but active transport happens only in living cells. A root taking up minerals from the soil is also active transport.

cards.p: Large substances are carried in vesicles made from the membrane, using ATP. Taking substances in is called endocytosis. Taking in solids is phagocytosis, and taking in fluids is pinocytosis. Sending substances out is called exocytosis.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><ellipse cx='57' cy='56' rx='16' ry='9' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c2)'/><g fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='3'><path d='M10,90 L30,90 C30,60 35,42 45,38'/><path d='M105,90 L85,90 C85,60 80,42 70,38'/><path d='M110,70 L145,70 C145,100 175,100 175,70 L210,70'/><path d='M215,70 L245,70'/><path d='M275,70 L310,70'/><path d='M245,70 C245,95 275,95 275,70'/></g><g fill='var(--c1)'><circle cx='160' cy='82' r='3'/><circle cx='152' cy='77' r='3'/><circle cx='168' cy='79' r='3'/><circle cx='130' cy='55' r='3'/><circle cx='190' cy='58' r='3'/></g><g fill='var(--c4)'><circle cx='260' cy='80' r='3.5'/><circle cx='254' cy='58' r='3.5'/><circle cx='268' cy='46' r='3.5'/><circle cx='262' cy='34' r='3.5'/></g><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='57' y='125'>Phagocytosis</text><text x='160' y='125'>Pinocytosis</text><text x='262' y='125'>Exocytosis</text></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='57' y='143'>solid particle</text><text x='160' y='143'>fluid droplet</text><text x='262' y='143'>secretion out</text></g><line x1='15' y1='155' x2='205' y2='155' stroke='var(--line)'/><text x='110' y='170' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Endocytosis (taking in)</text><text x='262' y='170' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>sending out</text><text x='160' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Top: outside the cell · Bottom: inside the cell · ATP is used</text></svg>
cards.key: Insulin secretion is an example of exocytosis. Exocytosis enlarges the membrane, and endocytosis shrinks it. Transport by vesicles happens only in living cells.

once.soru: How does a white blood cell take in a bacterium?

secenekler.yazi: It wraps it in membrane, in a vesicle
secenekler.neden: A bacterium is too big to pass through any channel. The white blood cell wraps it in membrane and takes it in inside a vesicle.
Channels are for small particles such as ions and water. A bacterium is much bigger.
Only small particles cross the membrane by diffusion. A bacterium can't seep through.

cards.p:
• The membrane has a fluid mosaic structure and is selectively permeable.
• Diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis are passive transport. Substances move from high to low, and no ATP is used.
• In active transport, substances are moved from low to high. Proteins and ATP are needed.
• Large substances are carried in vesicles by endocytosis and exocytosis.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><g stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'><line x1='160' y1='40' x2='80' y2='70'/><line x1='160' y1='40' x2='240' y2='70'/></g><rect x='105' y='14' width='110' height='28' rx='8' fill='var(--acc)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--acc)'/><text x='160' y='33' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Membrane transport</text><rect x='20' y='70' width='120' height='28' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c1)'/><rect x='180' y='70' width='120' height='28' rx='8' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c2)'/><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='80' y='89'>Passive: no ATP</text><text x='240' y='89'>Active: uses ATP</text></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='80' y='122'>diffusion</text><text x='80' y='142'>facilitated diff.</text><text x='80' y='162'>osmosis</text><text x='240' y='122'>pumps (Na-K)</text><text x='240' y='142'>endocytosis</text><text x='240' y='162'>exocytosis</text></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='80' y='188'>high to low</text><text x='240' y='188'>low to high / vesicle</text></g></svg>

quiz.q: Which kinds of transport use ATP? Put each one in the right group.
quiz.e: Diffusion, osmosis and facilitated diffusion happen on their own, from high to low. The Na-K pump moves substances from low to high, and phagocytosis and exocytosis form vesicles. These three use ATP.

quiz.q: A plant cell has an osmotic pressure of 12 atm and a turgor pressure of 5 atm. What is its suction force in atm?
quiz.e: Suction force is osmotic pressure minus turgor pressure: 12 − 5 = 7 atm. As the cell takes in water, turgor rises and suction force falls.

quiz.q: Put in order what happens to a plant cell placed in salt water.
ogeler: The outside becomes hypertonic to the cell
Water leaves the vacuole by osmosis
The vacuole shrinks and turgor pressure drops
The membrane pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis)
quiz.e: When the outside is more concentrated, water leaves the cell, the vacuole shrinks and turgor is lost. Finally the membrane pulls away from the wall. If the cell is put in pure water, the process reverses. This is called deplasmolysis.

quiz.q: Match each event with its kind of transport.
ciftler: A white blood cell engulfing a bacterium
A cell taking in a fluid droplet
quiz.e: Engulfing a solid particle is called phagocytosis, and taking in a fluid droplet is called pinocytosis. A vesicle fusing with the membrane and emptying its contents is called exocytosis. The diffusion of water across the membrane is osmosis.

fotosentez.title: Photosynthesis and chemosynthesis
fotosentez.summary: How does light energy become food, and how do producers that get no light survive?

cards.h: Photosynthesis: the equation and why it matters
cards.p: Plants, algae and cyanobacteria use light energy to make glucose from CO₂ and water. Along the way, O₂ is released. In this way, light energy becomes chemical bond energy.

cards.p: The chloroplast is an organelle with a double membrane. The flat sacs inside it are called thylakoids, and their stacks are called grana. Chlorophyll is found in the thylakoid membrane. The fluid around the thylakoids is called the stroma, and the Calvin cycle takes place there.

cards.key: The plural of granum is grana. Cyanobacteria have no chloroplasts. Their chlorophyll is in thylakoid membranes inside the cell.

etk.soru: Tap the parts of the chloroplast.

noktalar.acik: The chloroplast has a double membrane. The membranes control what goes in and out.
A granum is a stack of thylakoids piled on top of each other. The plural is grana, and the grana are linked to each other by stroma thylakoids.
A thylakoid is a flat sac. Its membrane holds chlorophyll, and the light-dependent reactions happen here.
The stroma is the fluid around the thylakoids. Here the Calvin cycle turns CO<sub>2</sub> into glucose.
The chloroplast has its own circular DNA. It makes some of its proteins itself.
The chloroplast's own ribosomes make proteins from the genes in its own DNA.

once.soru: Does the chloroplast have its own DNA?

secenekler.neden: The stroma contains its own DNA and ribosomes. It makes some of its proteins itself.
DNA is not found only in the nucleus. Chloroplasts and mitochondria have it too.
The chloroplast has both DNA and ribosomes.

cards.p: Chlorophyll a is the main pigment, found in the reaction center. Chlorophyll b and carotenoids capture light of other colors and pass the energy on to chlorophyll a.

once.soru: Why do leaves turn yellow in autumn?

secenekler.neden: When chlorophyll breaks down, the yellow and orange carotenoids that were in the leaf all along become visible.

secenekler.yazi: A new yellow pigment is made
secenekler.neden: The yellow pigments are in the leaf in summer too, but chlorophyll hides them.
Drying comes later. The color change starts when chlorophyll breaks down.

cards.p: An absorption spectrum shows how much of each color a pigment absorbs. Chlorophyll absorbs blue-violet and red light and reflects green light. An action spectrum shows how fast photosynthesis goes in different colors.

cards.p: The light-dependent reactions happen in the thylakoid membrane. Chlorophyll excited by light loses electrons, and the photolysis of water replaces them. Along the way, O₂ is released. This stage produces ATP and NADPH.

once.soru: Why is water split in the light-dependent stage?

secenekler.neden: Chlorophyll excited by light loses electrons, and the photolysis of water replaces them. O₂ is a by-product.
Glucose is made in the Calvin cycle in the stroma.
CO₂ binds to RuBP in the Calvin cycle. It does not combine with water.

cards.p: Light is captured by photosystem II and photosystem I. Noncyclic electron flow produces ATP, NADPH and O₂. In cyclic flow, only photosystem I works, and only ATP is made.

once.soru: In some light reactions, an electron returns to the same photosystem without involving water at all. Is O₂ released along this path?

secenekler.neden: Water is not split, so no O₂ is released. Only ATP is made.
O₂ is released only when water is split. This path does not use water.
Water is not used, so no O₂ is released at all.

cards.p: The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma. CO₂ is attached to 5-carbon RuBP by the enzyme rubisco. The PGA that forms is reduced to PGAL using ATP and NADPH. Most of the PGAL is used to remake RuBP.

cards.p: As light intensity and the amount of CO₂ increase, the rate of photosynthesis first rises, then levels off. The rate is highest at the optimum temperature. At higher temperatures, enzymes break down. The rate is low in green light.

cards.p: The rate of photosynthesis is set by the scarcest factor. On the flat part of the graph, adding more light does not help, but adding CO₂ raises the curve. When water runs short, the stomata close and CO₂ intake drops.

cards.key: Mg and N are part of the structure of chlorophyll. When they are lacking, leaves turn yellow. The amounts of chlorophyll and enzymes, the number of stomata and the leaf's structure are internal factors that also affect the rate.

cards.p: Some bacteria and archaea do not use light. Instead, they oxidize inorganic substances and use the energy released to make organic matter from CO₂. This is called chemosynthesis.

cards.key: Nitrifying bacteria enrich the soil by turning ammonia into nitrite and nitrite into nitrate. Chemosynthesis is found only in prokaryotes, and it produces no O₂.

once.soru: At deep-sea vents that get no light at all, who starts the food chain?

secenekler.neden: These bacteria get energy by oxidizing substances such as H₂S and make food from CO₂.
Mosses need light, and there is no light there.
The area around the vents is full of worms, mussels and crabs.

cards.p: In hot, dry weather, the stomata close and photosynthesis becomes less efficient. C4 plants first hold CO₂ in a 4-carbon compound. CAM plants open their stomata at night and store CO₂.

once.soru: When does a cactus open its stomata?

secenekler.neden: If a cactus opened its stomata during the day, it would lose a lot of water. So it takes in CO₂ at night and stores it.
In the desert, stomata left open during the day lose a lot of water.
The stomata have to open for the plant to take in CO₂.

cards.p:
• Glucose is made from CO₂ and water using light energy. The O₂ released comes from water.
• In the thylakoid, light energy produces ATP, NADPH and O₂.
• The Calvin cycle in the stroma uses these to turn CO₂ into glucose.
• The scarcest factor limits the rate.
• In chemosynthesis, the energy comes from oxidizing inorganic substances.

quiz.q: Group each event by the stage of photosynthesis it happens in.
quiz.e: In the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid, water is split, O₂ is released and ATP and NADPH are made. The Calvin cycle in the stroma attaches CO₂ to RuBP, reduces PGA to PGAL using ATP and NADPH and regenerates RuBP.

quiz.q: How many ATP are used in the Calvin cycle to make 3 glucose?
quiz.e: One glucose uses 18 ATP. So 3 glucose need 3 × 18 = 54 ATP.

quiz.q: Sort each feature into photosynthesis, chemosynthesis or both.
quiz.e: In photosynthesis, the energy comes from light and water is split. In chemosynthesis, the energy comes from oxidizing inorganic substances. Nitrifying bacteria are an example. In both, the producer makes organic matter from CO₂.

quiz.q: A plant was given CO₂ whose oxygen was labeled with ¹⁸O. Where does the labeled oxygen show up?
o: Only in the O₂ released
In the O₂ released and in glucose
Only in the water that reacts
In glucose and in the water formed
quiz.e: The O₂ released comes from the photolysis of water. The oxygen of CO₂ goes into glucose and into the water formed at the end of the reaction.
y: The O₂ released comes from splitting water. The oxygen of CO₂ goes into glucose and the water formed.
O₂ comes from the photolysis of water, not from CO₂. The labeled oxygen is found in glucose and in the water formed.
The oxygen of CO₂ does not go into the water that reacts. In the Calvin cycle, it goes into glucose and the water formed.

hucresel-solunum.title: Cellular respiration
hucresel-solunum.summary: How does a cell transfer the energy in food to ATP?

cards.h: The structure and cycle of ATP
cards.p: ATP is made of adenine, ribose and three phosphates. When the last phosphate is split off by hydrolysis, energy is released and ATP becomes ADP. When a phosphate is added back to ADP, ATP forms again.

cards.key: Active transport and synthesis reactions also run on ATP. The energy comes from the whole hydrolysis reaction, not just from breaking the bond.

once.soru: When a muscle contracts, which molecule directly supplies the energy it uses?

secenekler.neden: The energy of glucose is first transferred to ATP. The muscle then spends this ATP.
Glucose is not used directly. Its energy is first transferred to ATP.
O₂ does not supply energy. In respiration it acts as the electron acceptor.

cards.p: Adding a phosphate to ADP is called phosphorylation. In substrate-level phosphorylation, the phosphate comes from an organic molecule. Oxidative phosphorylation uses the energy of the electron transport chain (ETC), and photophosphorylation uses the energy of light.

once.soru: What is it called when a chloroplast makes ATP with light energy?

secenekler.neden: Photophosphorylation uses light energy and happens in the chloroplast during photosynthesis.
Oxidative phosphorylation happens in the mitochondrion, using the energy of the ETC.
Substrate-level phosphorylation is the transfer of a phosphate from an organic molecule to ADP.

cards.p: In aerobic respiration, glucose is broken down completely: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and the ETC in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

once.soru: How many turns does the Krebs cycle make for one glucose?

secenekler.neden: Glucose gives two pyruvates, and those give two acetyl-CoA.
One glucose gives two acetyl-CoA, and each one turns the cycle once.
Glucose has 6 carbons, but the cycle takes in acetyl groups two carbons at a time.

cards.p: In the inner mitochondrial membrane, NADH and FADH₂ hand their electrons to a chain. The energy of these electrons pumps H⁺ ions. As the H⁺ ions flow back through ATP synthase, ATP is made. The final electron acceptor is O₂.

once.soru: What does the oxygen we breathe do in the cell?

secenekler.neden: At the end of the ETC, O₂ takes the electrons and H⁺ ions and forms water.
Blood carries glucose. O₂ works in the ETC.
The CO₂ we breathe out comes from the carbons of glucose. O₂ becomes water.

cards.p: Most ATP is made in the ETC. One NADH gives about 2.5 ATP and one FADH₂ about 1.5 ATP. This makes a total of about 30-32 ATP. Older textbooks give this number as 36-38.

etk.soru: Change the ATP value used for one NADH and one FADH<sub>2</sub>. One glucose gives 10 NADH, 2 FADH<sub>2</sub> and 4 ATP directly.
yorum: With current values you get at most 32 ATP. Depending on how the NADH from glycolysis enters the mitochondrion, the result is about 30-32 ATP.
Current and older values are mixed here.
This is the older textbook count, which gives 36-38 ATP.

once.soru: Each glucose makes 10 NADH. If one NADH gives about 2.5 ATP, how much ATP comes from the NADH?

secenekler.neden: Each NADH gives more than one ATP.
That is the ATP from just one NADH.

cards.p: Without O₂, NAD⁺ runs out and glycolysis stops. In fermentation, pyruvate is reduced by NADH, which regenerates NAD⁺. This keeps glycolysis going. But ATP comes only from glycolysis, so the yield is a net 2 ATP.

cards.key: Fermentation takes place in the cytoplasm. Some books also call fermentation "anaerobic respiration". However, the anaerobic respiration of some bacteria does use an ETC.

cards.p: In alcoholic fermentation, yeast turns pyruvate into ethyl alcohol and CO₂. This CO₂ is what makes dough rise. Lactic acid fermentation is carried out by yogurt bacteria and tired muscle cells, and it produces lactic acid.

cards.key: The alcohol in dough evaporates in the oven. Lactic acid fermentation releases no CO₂. The muscle soreness you feel the next day comes from small injuries in the muscle, not from lactic acid.

etk.soru: Does each feature belong to aerobic respiration, to fermentation, or to both?
ogeler: Product is alcohol or lactic acid
All of fermentation happens in the cytoplasm, and mitochondria are not used.
Yeast can do both depending on conditions. With O<sub>2</sub> it respires aerobically, and without it, it ferments.

cards.h: Fats and proteins are burned too
cards.p: Cells also use fats and proteins for energy. Glycerol joins glycolysis, and fatty acids enter the Krebs cycle as acetyl-CoA. Amino acids first lose their nitrogen group, and the rest enters the Krebs pathway.

once.soru: Which gives the most energy per gram?

secenekler.neden: Fat gives about 9 kcal per gram. Carbohydrate and protein give about 4 kcal.
Carbohydrate gives about 4 kcal per gram. That is less than half of what fat gives.
Protein gives about 4 kcal per gram. That is less than half of what fat gives.

cards.p: Photosynthesis stores light energy in glucose. Respiration breaks this glucose down and transfers its energy to ATP. The products of one are the inputs of the other. Plants respire day and night.

cards.p:
• ATP gives energy by turning into ADP and phosphate. It is the energy currency of the cell.
• Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the matrix, and the ETC in the inner membrane.
• The final electron acceptor is O₂, and the total is about 30-32 ATP.
• Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ and gives a net 2 ATP.
• Photosynthesis and respiration produce each other's inputs.

quiz.q: Group each event by where it happens in the cell.
quiz.e: Glycolysis and fermentation happen in the cytoplasm. The Krebs cycle, including the formation of citrate from acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate, runs in the mitochondrial matrix. The ETC and ATP synthase work in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

quiz.q: A muscle cell breaks down 4 glucose by aerobic respiration and 6 glucose by lactic acid fermentation. If aerobic respiration gives 30 ATP per glucose, how much net ATP does the cell gain in total?
quiz.e: Aerobic respiration gives 4 × 30 = 120 ATP. Fermentation gives only the net 2 ATP of glycolysis per glucose: 6 × 2 = 12 ATP. The total is 132 ATP.

quiz.q: Put in order what happens to a glucose in aerobic respiration.
ogeler: Glucose splits into two pyruvates in the cytoplasm
CO₂ is removed from pyruvate and acetyl-CoA forms
Acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetate and citrate forms
NADH and FADH₂ from the Krebs cycle give electrons to the ETC
H⁺ is pumped into the intermembrane space
ATP is made as H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase
quiz.e: The order is glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, the Krebs cycle and the ETC. In the ETC, the energy of the electrons pumps H⁺. ATP is made as the H⁺ ions flow back through ATP synthase.

quiz.q: In a closed container with glucose, yeast first uses up the O₂ inside. What is observed after the O₂ runs out completely?
o: CO₂ release stops completely.
Lactic acid builds up.
Water formation in the ETC speeds up.
CO₂ release continues and ethyl alcohol builds up.
quiz.e: When the O₂ runs out, yeast switches to alcoholic fermentation. CO₂ release continues and alcohol builds up. Because the ETC stops, water formation there stops too.
y: Without oxygen, yeast switches to fermentation. Alcoholic fermentation also releases CO₂.
Yeast does alcoholic fermentation, not lactic acid fermentation. Lactic acid fermentation is seen in muscle cells and yogurt bacteria.
When the O₂ runs out, the ETC has no final electron acceptor. Water formation stops and fermentation begins.

mitoz.title: Mitosis and asexual reproduction
mitoz.summary: How does a cell split in two, and how do living things multiply from a single parent?

cards.h: The cell cycle: interphase and M
cards.p: The time from a cell's formation to its division is called the cell cycle. The longest stage is interphase. The cell grows in G1, copies its DNA in S and prepares to divide in G2. Then come mitosis and cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm.

cards.p: The loose DNA in interphase is called chromatin. During division, chromatin shortens and thickens and is then called a chromosome. A copied chromosome is made of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. In humans, 2n = 46.

cards.h: Metaphase: a single line at the equator
cards.p: In metaphase, spindle fibers attach to the centromeres, and the chromosomes line up in a single row at the equator. As you just found, the chromosomes are at their shortest and most distinct in this stage. That is why a karyotype is made in this stage.

once.soru: What is pulled to opposite poles in anaphase?

secenekler.neden: Once the centromere splits, each chromatid is pulled to its own pole.
The nuclear envelope already disappeared in prophase.
The centrosomes are already at the poles. What gets pulled to the poles are the chromatids.

cards.p: In telophase, the chromosomes loosen and the nuclear envelope forms again. Then the cytoplasm divides. This is called cytokinesis. An animal cell divides by pinching in at the middle. A plant cell builds a cell plate in the middle.

once.soru: A human cell with 2n = 46 divided by mitosis. How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell?

secenekler.neden: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same. A 2n cell gives 2n cells again.
The division that halves the chromosome number is meiosis.
92 chromosomes are seen only for a short time, in anaphase.

cards.h: Why mitosis matters and how it is controlled
cards.p: Mitosis allows growth, repair and renewal. In single-celled eukaryotes, it is also a way to reproduce. The cycle has checkpoints at G1, G2 and metaphase. If this control breaks down, cancer can develop.

cards.key: As a cell grows, its surface-to-volume ratio drops and division begins. Mature nerve cells do not divide.

once.soru: Which kind of division closes a cut on your hand?

secenekler.neden: The skin cells at the edge of the wound divide by mitosis and fill the gap.
Meiosis only makes reproductive cells.
Cells cannot fill the gap just by growing. New cells are needed.

cards.p: In asexual reproduction, a single parent is enough and there is no fertilization. The offspring are genetically identical to the parent. Amoebas and euglenas divide by mitosis. A bacterium's binary fission is not mitosis, because a bacterium has no nucleus.

once.soru: An outgrowth forms on a yeast cell, grows and breaks off. What kind of reproduction is this?

secenekler.neden: A small bud grows on the parent. The offspring is smaller than the parent.
In fission, the parent splits in two and the two offspring are about equal.
A spore is a single cell, and many of them form inside sacs.

cards.p: Regrowing a lost part is called regeneration. If the broken-off piece becomes a whole individual, it counts as reproduction. Planarians reproduce this way. In parthenogenesis, an unfertilized egg develops. Male honeybees (n) form this way.

once.soru: A lizard regrows its lost tail. Is this reproduction?

secenekler.neden: No new individual forms. Only the lost part is regrown.
Reproduction requires a new individual. The tail does not become an individual.

secenekler.yazi: Yes, if the tail is long
secenekler.neden: The length of the tail does not matter, because no new individual forms.

cards.p: Plants can make new individuals from their roots, stems or leaves. Willows are grown from cuttings, grapevines by layering and fruit trees by grafting. Potatoes spread by tubers, onions by bulbs and strawberries by runners.

cards.p: In tissue culture, a few plant cells grow into a whole plant in a sterile medium. In cloning, the nucleus of a body cell is moved into an egg whose nucleus has been removed. Dolly the sheep was born this way in 1996.

once.soru: Dolly's nuclear DNA is the same as which sheep's?

secenekler.neden: The nucleus moved into the egg carries all of Dolly's nuclear DNA.
The egg's nucleus had been removed.
The surrogate mother only grows the embryo.

cards.p:
• The cell cycle is made of interphase (G1, S, G2), mitosis and cytokinesis. DNA is copied in the S phase.
• Chromosomes appear in prophase, line up at the equator in metaphase, chromatids separate in anaphase and nuclei form in telophase.
• Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same.
• In asexual reproduction, the offspring are usually identical to the parent.

quiz.q: Put the events in an animal cell's cycle in order.
ogeler: Chromosomes appear and the nuclear envelope disappears
Chromosomes line up in a single row at the equator
Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles
The nuclear envelope forms again at the poles
The cytoplasm pinches in and divides
quiz.e: DNA is copied in the S phase of interphase. Then chromosomes appear in prophase, line up at the equator in metaphase and their chromatids separate in anaphase. Nuclei form in telophase, and cytokinesis comes last.

quiz.q: A human cell with 2n = 46 chromosomes is going through mitosis. How many chromatids does this cell have in metaphase?
quiz.e: In the S phase, every chromosome is copied and carries two sister chromatids. That is why there are 46 × 2 = 92 chromatids.

quiz.q: Match each example with its type of asexual reproduction.
ciftler: A piece of planarian becoming an individual
quiz.e: An amoeba divides by mitosis, yeast buds and bread mold makes spores in a sporangium. A cut piece of planarian becomes a whole individual by regeneration. A male honeybee develops from an unfertilized egg. This is called parthenogenesis.

quiz.q: In a cell going through mitosis, which of these shows that it is a plant cell?
o: Spindle fibers forming
Chromosomes lining up at the equator
Sister chromatids separating
The cytoplasm dividing with a cell plate
quiz.e: Spindle fibers forming, chromosomes lining up at the equator and chromatids separating happen in both kinds of cell. A cell plate, however, forms only in plant cells.
y: Spindle fibers also form in animal cells. What is unique to plants is division with a cell plate.
Chromosomes line up at the equator in every mitosis. What is unique to plants is the cell plate.
Sister chromatids separate in the anaphase of every mitosis. What marks a plant is the cytoplasm dividing with a cell plate.

mayoz.title: Meiosis and sexual reproduction
mayoz.summary: How is the chromosome number halved, and where does variety come from?

cards.p: If gametes carried as many chromosomes as body cells, the chromosome number would double in every generation. Meiosis halves the chromosome number (2n → n). In animals it makes gametes, and in plants it makes spores.

cards.p: In a diploid cell, every chromosome has a partner. One comes from the mother and the other from the father. These partners are called homologous chromosomes. Homologs have the same length, shape and order of genes. Humans have 23 homologous pairs.

once.soru: Of the 46 chromosomes in a human body cell, how many come from the mother?

secenekler.neden: One of each pair comes from the mother and the other from the father.
Not all 46 chromosomes come from a single parent.
Half of them come from the mother.

cards.p: Before meiosis, DNA is copied once. In prophase I, homologous chromosomes line up side by side along their whole length. This is called synapsis. The structure of four chromatids is called a tetrad. Tetrads do not form in mitosis.

once.soru: When a germ cell completes meiosis, how many cells form?

secenekler.neden: Two divisions come one after the other. One cell first becomes two, then four.
In meiosis, the cell divides twice. That is why four cells form, not two.
DNA is copied once, but the cell divides twice. The result is 4 cells.

cards.h: DNA and chromosome number in meiosis
cards.p: In a cell with 2n = 4, the amount of DNA rises from 2 units to 4 units in the S phase. It drops to 2 units in telophase I and to 1 unit in telophase II. The number of chromosomes drops from 4 to 2 in meiosis I.

once.soru: In which division of meiosis is the chromosome number halved?

secenekler.neden: When the homologs separate, each cell gets only one of each pair. This drops the number from 2n to n.
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids. By this stage, the chromosome number is already n.
The chromosome number is halved only once, in meiosis I.

cards.p: Both mitosis and meiosis start with DNA copying. Mitosis allows growth, repair and asexual reproduction, and it keeps the chromosome number the same. Meiosis makes gametes or spores, halves the chromosome number and creates variety.

cards.p: There are three sources of variety. The first is crossing over. The second is the independent assortment of homologs in metaphase I. This creates 2n kinds of gametes, and in humans that number is about 8.4 million. The third is the random joining of gametes at fertilization.

cards.p: The nondisjunction you just saw leads to gametes with n+1 and n−1 chromosomes. In Down syndrome, there are three copies of chromosome 21, and the total chromosome number is 47. This risk rises as the mother gets older.

cards.p: In males, one germ cell gives four equal cells, which means four sperm. This is called spermatogenesis. In females, the cytoplasm does not divide equally. One large egg and small polar bodies form. This is called oogenesis.

once.soru: How many eggs does one egg mother cell give through meiosis?

secenekler.neden: The cytoplasm does not divide equally. One cell becomes the egg, and the others become small polar bodies.
In males four sperm form, but in females only one egg forms.
The polar bodies do not become eggs. Only one egg forms.

cards.p: The joining of the sperm and egg nuclei is called fertilization. Two n gametes join and form a 2n zygote. In fish and frogs, external fertilization happens in water. In reptiles, birds and mammals, internal fertilization happens inside the female's body.

etk.soru: Sort each animal by how fertilization happens.
ogeler: A frog releases its eggs and sperm into water. Fertilization happens outside the body.
A dolphin lives in water, but it is a mammal. Fertilization happens inside the female's body.

once.soru: How many sets of chromosomes does the zygote formed by fertilization carry?

secenekler.neden: A sperm (n) and an egg (n) join. So n + n = 2n.
Gametes are the ones with n chromosomes. A zygote forms when two gametes join.
Each gamete brings one set of chromosomes. That makes two sets in total.

cards.p: In asexual reproduction, a single parent gives offspring like itself. This is fast, but there is little variety. Sexual reproduction involves meiosis and fertilization. The offspring differ both from their parents and from one another.

once.soru: If conditions suddenly change, which population has a better chance of survival?

secenekler.neden: The offspring differ from one another. That is why some of them can adapt to the new conditions.
The individuals are nearly all the same, so one change affects them all at once.
Variety is a big advantage in a changing environment.

cards.p:
• In meiosis, DNA is copied once, the cell divides twice and 4 different n cells form.
• Homologs separate in meiosis I, and sister chromatids separate in meiosis II.
• Variety comes from crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilization.
• Nondisjunction leads to outcomes such as Down syndrome.
• In plants, spores form by meiosis and gametes by mitosis.

quiz.q: Put the events of meiosis in order.
ogeler: Homologs pair up into tetrads and cross over
Tetrads line up in pairs at the equator
Homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles
Sister chromatids move to opposite poles
quiz.e: DNA is copied once before meiosis. In prophase I, tetrads form and crossing over happens. In metaphase I the tetrads line up in pairs, and in anaphase I the homologs separate. In anaphase II the sister chromatids separate, and four n cells form.

quiz.q: In an organism with 2n = 8, the homologs differ from each other and there is no crossing over. How many kinds of gametes can form by independent assortment?
quiz.e: The number of homologous pairs is n = 4. Independent assortment gives 2<sup>4</sup> = 16 kinds of gametes.

quiz.q: Sort each event by the division it happens in.
ogeler: Can happen in a haploid cell
quiz.e: Tetrads, crossing over and homologs separating are unique to meiosis. A haploid cell can only go through mitosis, and mitosis gives identical cells. DNA copying, centromeres splitting and spindle fibers are found in both divisions.

quiz.q: In a human (2n = 46), meiosis I goes normally. In meiosis II, the sister chromatids of one chromosome fail to separate in just one of the two cells. What are the chromosome numbers of the four gametes?
quiz.e: At the end of meiosis I, both cells have 23 chromosomes. The cell with nondisjunction gives gametes with 24 and 22 chromosomes, and the normal cell gives gametes with 23 and 23.
y: This pattern belongs to nondisjunction in meiosis I. In meiosis II, only one cell is affected.
The two gametes from the cell with nondisjunction cannot be normal. One gets an extra chromosome, and the other is missing one.
Gametes are haploid. 47 and 45 chromosomes can only appear after fertilization, in the zygote.

kalitim.title: Heredity (Mendelian genetics)
kalitim.summary: How are traits passed from generation to generation? The rules of heredity, from Mendel to the family tree

olay.h: 28,000 pea plants in a monastery garden
olay.p: For eight years, Gregor Mendel grew about 28,000 pea plants and counted their flowers and seeds one by one. The ratios he counted came out the same every time.

cards.p: A piece of DNA that determines a trait is called a gene, and the gene's position on a chromosome is called its locus. The different forms of a gene are called alleles (such as A and a). If the alleles are the same, the individual is homozygous (AA, aa). If they differ, it is heterozygous (Aa).

once.soru: How many alleles for the eye color gene are in one of your body cells?

secenekler.neden: Each homologous chromosome carries one allele. One comes from the mother and the other from the father.
A gamete has one allele, while a body cell has two.
There is one on each homologous chromosome, so there are two alleles in total.

cards.p: An individual's pair of alleles is called its genotype, and the trait you can see is called its phenotype. In an Aa individual, the allele that shows its effect is dominant (A), and the hidden allele is recessive (a). A recessive trait appears only in aa individuals.

cards.key: Being dominant does not mean being more common or stronger. For example, having six fingers (polydactyly) is a dominant trait, but it is rare.

once.soru: If brown eyes (A) are dominant over blue (a), what color are the eyes of a person with genotype Aa?

secenekler.neden: The dominant A allele masks the effect of the a allele.
Blue eyes appear only in people with genotype aa.
With complete dominance, no in-between color forms.

cards.p: In the 1860s, Mendel made thousands of crosses with peas. Peas produce many seeds and fertilize themselves to give true-breeding lines. Also, seven of their traits come in two clear forms.

cards.h: The law of segregation and the Punnett square
cards.p: The parents are called P, the offspring F1 and the grandchildren F2. When gametes form, the alleles of a gene pair separate from each other. This is called the law of segregation. By the Punnett square, an Aa × Aa cross gives a genotype ratio of 1:2:1 and a phenotype ratio of 3:1.

cards.p: In the test cross you just made, an individual with the dominant phenotype is crossed with aa. If all the offspring have the dominant phenotype, the individual is most likely AA. If half the offspring are recessive, the individual is Aa.

etk.soru: There is one gene with complete dominance. Match each cross with the phenotype of its offspring.

once.soru: How many kinds of gametes does an AaBb individual make?

secenekler.neden: One allele from each gene pair goes into a gamete. This gives the gametes AB, Ab, aB and ab.
The two genes sort independently, so the allele combinations multiply.
16 is the number of boxes when two AaBb individuals are crossed.

cards.p: In the incomplete dominance you just saw, a heterozygous individual shows an in-between phenotype. For example, an RW snapdragon has pink flowers. In codominance, the effects of both alleles show fully. For example, a person with genotype IAIB has blood type AB.

cards.h: How sex is determined in humans
cards.p: Humans have 44 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes. Women are XX, and men are XY. All eggs carry an X chromosome. Half of the sperm carry an X, and half carry a Y. That is why the sperm determines the sex.

cards.key: Earlier children do not change the probability. Even after three girls, the chance of a boy is ½.

once.soru: A couple has three daughters. What is the chance that their fourth child is a boy?

secenekler.neden: Each birth is independent of the others. A sperm has an even chance of carrying an X or a Y.
Earlier children do not change the probability.
The chance is ½ again with every birth.

cards.p: Color blindness and hemophilia are passed on by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A woman with genotype XHXh is healthy, but she is a carrier. A man has only one X, so a single recessive allele is enough. That is why these conditions are more common in men.

once.soru: A gene on the Y chromosome passes from a father to whom?

secenekler.neden: Every son gets a Y chromosome from his father.
Daughters get an X from their father, not a Y.
Daughters have no Y chromosome.

cards.p: Genes on the same chromosome are usually passed on together. They are called linked genes. An AB/ab individual mostly makes AB and ab gametes. If crossing over happens, a small number of Ab and aB gametes also form.

once.soru: How do two genes that sit next to each other on the same chromosome sort into gametes?

secenekler.neden: They are carried on the same chromosome, so they do not sort independently.
Independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes.
Crossing over sometimes separates these genes.

cards.p: Traits such as height and skin color are set by many genes together. This is called polygenic inheritance. Together with the effect of the environment, it gives a smooth range from short to tall. The sources of variety are crossing over, independent assortment, random fertilization and mutation.

once.soru: Why do the heights of students in a class vary smoothly from short to tall?

secenekler.neden: The number of active alleles and environmental effects such as nutrition create a smooth range.
If one gene set the trait, there would be only a few clear groups.
Height is strongly inherited, but no single gene sets it.

cards.p: In a family tree, a square shows a male, a circle shows a female and a filled symbol shows an affected individual. If two healthy parents have an affected child, the trait is recessive. Marriage between relatives raises the risk of recessive conditions.

once.soru: Two healthy parents have an albino child. What kind of trait is albinism?

secenekler.neden: The parents are carriers (Aa). The child got both recessive alleles.
If albinism were dominant, at least one parent would be albino.
Albinism is a trait passed on through genes.

cards.p: The phenotype is the result of the genotype and the environment working together. A change the environment makes without changing the DNA is called a modification, and it is not inherited. A mutation is a lasting change in the DNA, and if it happens in a reproductive cell, it passes to the offspring.

once.soru: If someone gets a tan in the sun, will their children be born darker?

secenekler.neden: Tanning does not change the DNA. It is a modification and is not inherited.
A change the environment makes in the phenotype does not pass to the offspring.
A modification does not pass to any child.

cards.p:
• When gametes form, alleles separate. Genes on different chromosomes sort independently.
• An Aa × Aa cross gives a phenotype ratio of 3:1 and a genotype ratio of 1:2:1.
• n heterozygous pairs give 2n gametes.
• Incomplete dominance gives an in-between phenotype, and in codominance both alleles show together.
• X-linked recessive conditions are common in males.

quiz.q: The genes are on different chromosomes. In an AaBb × Aabb cross, what percent chance is there of an offspring with genotype aabb?
quiz.e: In Aa × Aa, the chance of aa is 1/4, and in Bb × bb, the chance of bb is 1/2. Multiply the two probabilities: 1/4 · 1/2 = 1/8, which is 12.5%.

quiz.q: The mother has type AB (I<sup>A</sup>I<sup>B</sup>), and the father has type O (ii). Which blood types can the children have?
quiz.e: The mother gives I<sup>A</sup> or I<sup>B</sup>, and the father gives only i. So the children have a ½ chance of I<sup>A</sup>i (A) and a ½ chance of I<sup>B</sup>i (B). Type AB needs two I alleles, and type O needs two i alleles. Neither is possible.

quiz.q: Which changes can pass to the offspring? Put each one in the right group.
ogeler: A mutation in a skin cell
quiz.e: Blood type and the hemophilia allele pass to the offspring through genes, and a mutation in a sperm passes on through the reproductive cell. Tanning and muscles growing with exercise are modifications that do not change the DNA. A mutation in a skin cell also stays in that individual only.

quiz.q: A girl is color-blind. Which statement about her family is certain?
o: Her father is color-blind.
Her mother is color-blind.
All her brothers are color-blind.
Her father is a carrier, and her mother is healthy.
quiz.e: Both of the girl's X chromosomes carry the recessive allele, and one of them came from her father. The father has only one X, so he is certainly color-blind. The mother may be a carrier or affected. Males cannot be carriers.
y: The girl gets one X from her father. The mother may not be color-blind and may only be a carrier.
Brothers get their X chromosome from the mother. If the mother is a carrier, only some of them may be color-blind.
A male has only one X, so a male cannot be a carrier. The father who gave his X to the girl is certainly color-blind.

dna-genetik-kod.title: DNA, replication and biotechnology
dna-genetik-kod.summary: The structure of DNA, how it is copied, mutations and biotechnology

cards.p: The building block of DNA is called a nucleotide. A nucleotide is made of a phosphate, a deoxyribose sugar and a base. The bases are A, G, T and C. The double-ringed A and G are called purines, and the single-ringed T and C are called pyrimidines.

cards.p: Starting from Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photo, Watson and Crick built the double helix model in 1953. DNA looks like a twisted ladder. The sides of the ladder are sugar-phosphate chains, and the rungs are base pairs.
cards.key: Nucleotides in the same strand are joined by phosphodiester bonds. In linear double-stranded DNA, the number of phosphodiester bonds is the number of nucleotides minus 2.

once.soru: If we compare the double helix to a twisted ladder, what do the rungs stand for?

secenekler.neden: The paired bases are the rungs that join the two strands.
The sugar-phosphate chains are the sides of the ladder.
The rungs are made of bases, not proteins.

cards.p: Paired bases hold on to each other with hydrogen bonds. There are two hydrogen bonds between A and T, and three between G and C. The two strands are antiparallel. One runs 5'→3', and the other runs 3'→5'.

cards.p: In double-stranded DNA, the number of adenines equals the number of thymines (A = T), and the number of guanines equals the number of cytosines (G = C). For example, if 200 base pairs contain 80 A, then T = 80, and G and C are 120 each.

once.soru: Which base is not found in RNA?

secenekler.neden: RNA has uracil (U) in place of thymine.
A, G and C are found in both DNA and RNA.
A, G and C are found in both DNA and RNA.

cards.p: A section of DNA that carries the information for a protein or an RNA is called a gene. DNA wraps around histone proteins to form chromatin. During division, chromatin packs tightly and is called a chromosome. All the genetic information of an organism is called its genome.

once.soru: What is the difference between chromatin and a chromosome?

secenekler.neden: Both are the same DNA. During division, chromatin packs tightly and becomes a chromosome.
The genes are the same. The only thing that changes is how tightly the DNA is packed.

secenekler.yazi: One is DNA, the other protein
secenekler.neden: Both are DNA wrapped around histones.

cards.p: After replication, each new DNA molecule has one old strand and one new strand. This is called semiconservative replication. In 1958, Meselson and Stahl showed this with bacteria they moved from a ¹⁵N medium to a ¹⁴N medium.

cards.p: DNA replication happens during interphase. Helicase separates the strands. Primase makes a short RNA primer. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the end of the primer and works only in the 5'→3' direction.

cards.p: As the replication fork opens, the leading strand grows continuously. The other strand is built in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, and ligase joins these pieces. This strand is called the lagging strand.

once.soru: DNA polymerase can build only in the 5'→3' direction. As the fork opens, how are the two strands built?

secenekler.neden: The strands are antiparallel. One is built continuously toward the fork, and the other is built backward in pieces.
The strands are antiparallel, so one has to be built in the direction away from the fork.
The strand that grows toward the fork can be built continuously.

cards.p: A lasting change in DNA is called a mutation. In a gene mutation, the bases change. Sickle-cell anemia is an example. In a chromosome mutation, a part of a chromosome or the number of chromosomes changes. Down syndrome is an example. Mutagens make mutations more likely.

once.soru: In Down syndrome, there are three copies of chromosome 21. What kind of mutation is this?

secenekler.neden: The chromosome number has changed. There are 47 chromosomes instead of 46.
Here it is not the bases of one gene that changed. A whole extra chromosome is present.
Every lasting change in DNA is a mutation.

cards.p: A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at specific places. The insulin gene is joined into a bacterium's plasmid with ligase, forming recombinant DNA. As the bacterium multiplies, it makes human insulin.

once.soru: Where is most of the human insulin used by people with diabetes made today?

secenekler.neden: The human insulin gene is moved into these organisms, and they make the insulin.
Getting insulin from blood would give small amounts and be expensive.
Insulin comes from genetically modified microbes, not from plants.

cards.p: PCR is a method for copying a piece of DNA in a tube, and the number of copies doubles with every cycle. DNA fingerprinting compares regions that are unique to each person. It is used in criminal cases and paternity tests.

once.soru: What do we call corn that has been given a bacterial gene to make it resistant to insects?

secenekler.neden: An organism that has received a gene from another species is called a genetically modified organism.
A clone is an exact copy of an organism. Here, a new gene has been added.
A hybrid comes from crossing two varieties, and no gene from another species is moved.

once.soru: A leukemia patient gets a bone marrow transplant. Which cells make the new blood cells?

secenekler.neden: Stem cells in the bone marrow divide and become blood cells.
Muscle cells are specialized and cannot make blood cells.
Nerve cells are specialized and are not found in bone marrow.

once.soru: What is the chance that a child of two carrier parents gets a recessive condition?

secenekler.neden: In an Aa × Aa cross, 1/4 of the children are aa.
1/2 is the chance that the child is a carrier (Aa).
The parents are not affected, but both carry the recessive allele.

cards.p:
• A nucleotide is made of a phosphate, deoxyribose and a base. There are 2 hydrogen bonds between A and T, and 3 between G and C.
• In double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C.
• Replication is semiconservative.
• Mutations happen at the gene or chromosome level.
• Biotechnology includes recombinant DNA, PCR, fingerprinting and cloning.

quiz.q: A double-stranded DNA of 2,000 nucleotides has 600 adenines. How many hydrogen bonds does this DNA have in total?
quiz.e: T = 600, and G and C are (2,000 − 1,200) / 2 = 400 each. The 600 A–T pairs make 2 bonds each, and the 400 G–C pairs make 3 bonds each. The total is 1,200 + 1,200 = 2,400 hydrogen bonds.

quiz.q: Put the events on the lagging strand during DNA replication in order.
ogeler: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds and separates the strands
Primase makes a short RNA primer
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the end of the primer
The RNA primers are removed and replaced with DNA
quiz.e: First, helicase separates the strands. Polymerase cannot start a chain from scratch, so primase makes a primer and polymerase extends it. Then the primers are replaced with DNA, and ligase joins the pieces.

quiz.q: Match each biotechnology term with its description.
ciftler: Cuts DNA at a specific sequence
Copies a piece of DNA in a tube
Compares regions unique to a person
A cell that has not yet specialized
quiz.e: A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at specific sequences. A plasmid is a bacterium's small, ring-shaped DNA. PCR copies a piece of DNA in a tube, and fingerprinting compares regions unique to a person. A stem cell is a cell that has not yet specialized.

quiz.q: A linear, double-stranded DNA is made of 1,200 nucleotides. How many phosphodiester bonds are there in total in the strands of this DNA?
quiz.e: Each strand is made of 600 nucleotides and has 599 phosphodiester bonds. The two strands have 2 · 599 = 1,198 bonds in total. One molecule of water was released as each bond formed.

protein-sentezi.title: Protein synthesis
protein-sentezi.summary: How does the code in a gene become a protein?

cards.h: From gene to protein: the central dogma
cards.p: A region of DNA that carries the instructions for making a protein is called a gene. This information is first copied into RNA. This is called transcription. Then it is translated into the language of amino acids. This is called translation.

cards.key: This flow of information from DNA to RNA and from RNA to protein is called the central dogma. Some genes code for RNA rather than protein.

cards.p: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter region at the start of the gene and opens the DNA. It reads only the template strand and extends the RNA in the 5'→3' direction. A U is placed opposite each A in the template.

cards.key: No primer is needed in this process. At the end region, the RNA comes off and the DNA closes again. The mRNA is a copy of the coding strand with U written in place of T.

once.soru: If the template DNA strand is 3'-TAC-5', what is the mRNA?

secenekler.neden: A pairs with T, U pairs with A and G pairs with C.
RNA has no T. U pairs with A.
This is a copy of the template. The mRNA is the complement of the template.

cards.p: In eukaryotes, transcription happens in the nucleus. Along the way, introns are cut out, exons are joined and the mRNA moves into the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes have no nucleus. That is why transcription and translation happen at the same time.

once.soru: In a bacterium, can ribosomes start reading an mRNA while it is still being written?

secenekler.neden: A bacterium has no nuclear envelope. So writing and reading happen in the same place at the same time.

secenekler.yazi: No, it must leave the nucleus
secenekler.neden: A bacterium has no nucleus.
Bacteria have ribosomes too, because every cell makes proteins.

cards.p: mRNA is read three bases at a time, with no gaps. Each triplet is called a codon, and there are 4³ = 64 codons. The AUG codon starts synthesis and codes for methionine. UAA, UAG and UGA stop synthesis.

cards.p: More than one codon can code for the same amino acid. That is why the genetic code is redundant. But a codon always stands for just one amino acid. The code is the same in nearly all living things, so it is universal.

once.soru: There are 64 codons, but only 20 amino acids. How is that possible?

secenekler.yazi: One amino acid can have several codons
secenekler.neden: For example, 6 different codons code for leucine. This is called a redundant code.

secenekler.yazi: Some codons code for two amino acids
secenekler.neden: A codon always stands for just one amino acid. Otherwise the protein would be ambiguous.

secenekler.yazi: The extra codons are not used
secenekler.neden: Each of the 61 codons codes for an amino acid, and the remaining 3 are stop codons.

cards.p: tRNA carries amino acids to the ribosome. One end of a tRNA holds a specific amino acid, and the other end has a three-base anticodon. The anticodon pairs with the codon on the mRNA.

once.soru: If the codon on the mRNA is AUG, what is the anticodon of the tRNA that pairs with it?

secenekler.neden: A pairs with U, U with A and G with C.
A sequence does not pair with itself. The anticodon must be complementary.
T is found only in DNA. tRNA has U.

cards.p: The ribosome is a structure without a membrane where translation takes place. The small subunit holds the mRNA. In the large subunit, peptide bonds form, and tRNAs sit in the A, P and E sites.

cards.key: A ribosome is made of rRNA and protein, and its subunits come together only during synthesis. A prokaryotic ribosome (70S) is smaller than a eukaryotic one (80S).

once.soru: If you compare a bacterium with a human cell, which one has ribosomes?

secenekler.neden: Ribosomes have no membrane and make proteins in both bacteria and human cells. A bacterial ribosome (70S) is smaller.
Bacteria make proteins too, and they have ribosomes.
In a human cell, ribosomes are found both in the cytoplasm and on the rough ER.

cards.p: The small subunit finds the AUG codon on the mRNA, and the initiator tRNA carrying methionine pairs with it. Then the large subunit joins. The initiator tRNA sits in the P site, and the A site stays empty.

once.soru: Which amino acid does the synthesis of every protein start with?

secenekler.neden: The start codon, AUG, codes for methionine.
The codons for leucine are not start codons.
The codons for glycine are not start codons.

cards.p: A new tRNA arrives at the A site. The chain in the P site is transferred to the amino acid in the A site by a peptide bond. Then the ribosome shifts by one codon, and the empty tRNA leaves from the E site.

cards.p: When a stop codon reaches the A site, there is no tRNA that pairs with it. Instead, a release factor binds and the chain is released. The subunits separate, and the polypeptide folds into a working protein.

once.soru: The UAA stop codon has reached the ribosome's A site. What happens now?

secenekler.neden: No tRNA comes to a stop codon. A protein factor binds and releases the chain.

secenekler.yazi: One more amino acid is added
secenekler.neden: A stop codon does not code for an amino acid.
The ribosome does not skip the stop codon. Synthesis ends there.

cards.p: Many ribosomes can read one mRNA at the same time. This is called a polyribosome. Free ribosomes make the proteins that will stay in the cytoplasm. Ribosomes on the rough ER make the proteins that will be secreted.

once.soru: A pancreas cell secretes insulin. On which ribosomes is insulin made?

secenekler.neden: Proteins to be secreted are made on rough ER ribosomes and packaged in the Golgi.
Free ribosomes make the proteins that stay inside the cell.
mRNA is written in the nucleus. Protein is made on ribosomes.

cards.p: The mRNA coding for a polypeptide of n amino acids has n + 1 codons, counting the stop codon. That makes 3(n + 1) nucleotides. The number of peptide bonds in the chain, and of water molecules released, is n − 1.

cards.p:
• Information flows from DNA to mRNA, and from mRNA to protein.
• In eukaryotes introns are removed, and in prokaryotes the two processes happen at the same time.
• 64 codons code for 20 amino acids. AUG starts, and stop codons end.
• n amino acids have n − 1 peptide bonds.
• A mutation can be silent, missense, nonsense or a frameshift.

etk.soru: Put the steps from gene to protein in a eukaryotic cell in order.

quiz.q: A mature mRNA codes for a single-chain polypeptide of 200 amino acids. How many nucleotides are in its coding region, counting the stop codon?
quiz.e: 200 amino acids need 200 codons, and with the stop codon there are 201 codons. 201 × 3 = 603 nucleotides.

quiz.q: The coding region of an mRNA is 612 nucleotides, counting the stop codon. How many tRNA molecules come to the ribosome while a polypeptide is made from this mRNA?
quiz.e: There are 612 / 3 = 204 codons. No tRNA comes to the stop codon, and one tRNA brings each of the 203 amino acids. So 203 tRNAs come.

quiz.q: Match each base change with its type of mutation. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.
quiz.e: If the same amino acid comes, the mutation is silent. If a different amino acid comes, it is missense. UGA is a stop codon, so the protein stays short. This is a nonsense mutation. When a nucleotide is deleted, every codon after it changes. This is called a frameshift.

quiz.q: The template strand of a gene has the sequence 3'-TAC GGA-5'. Which mRNA sequence is made from this region?
o: 5'-AUG CCU-3'
5'-ATG CCT-3'
5'-UAC GGA-3'
3'-AUG CCU-5'
quiz.e: The mRNA is complementary to the template strand and runs in the opposite direction. A pairs with T, U with A and C with G. RNA has no T.
y: mRNA has uracil in place of thymine. A sequence with T is DNA and cannot be RNA.
You wrote the same sequence as the template. The mRNA is complementary to the template. A pairs with T, U with A and C with G.
The bases are right, but the ends are reversed. The mRNA runs opposite to the template, so its 5' end is opposite TAC.

siniflandirma.title: Classifying living things
siniflandirma.summary: How are living things grouped, and how are species named?

cards.p: More than one and a half million species of living things have been named so far. Classification means grouping living things by shared traits. This makes it easier to identify them, see how they are related and share information.

once.soru: About how many species of living things have been named on Earth?

secenekler.neden: New species are found every year too. Memorizing so many species one by one is impossible. That is why we group living things.
There are more than 10,000 bird species alone.
The number of insect species alone is close to a million.

cards.p: Artificial classification looks at appearance. So it puts the bat and the eagle in a "flyers" group. Natural classification looks at relatedness and compares homologous organs, embryos and DNA. By this classification, the bat is a mammal.

once.soru: Both bats and eagles fly. But a bat gives birth to live young and feeds them milk. Which group does the bat belong to?

secenekler.neden: By natural classification, which looks at relatedness, the bat is a mammal. Its wing has the same origin as a human arm.
Flying is a shared job, but it does not show relatedness. Bats have no feathers and nurse their young.
A bat has a skeleton and is not closely related to insects.

cards.p: Living things are placed in nested levels. From broadest to narrowest, these levels are: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. The basic unit of classification is the species.

cards.h: What is a species? The mule example
cards.p: In sexually reproducing organisms, a species is made up of individuals that can mate with each other and produce fertile offspring. The fact that mules are sterile shows that horses and donkeys are separate species. In bacteria, species are told apart by their DNA.

cards.p: Linnaeus gave each species a two-word Latin name. First comes the genus name with a capital letter, then the species name in lowercase. The name is written in italics: Homo sapiens.

cards.p: Living things are first divided into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryotes. The first two are prokaryotes. But archaea are not bacteria and are more closely related to eukaryotes.

cards.key: There are six kingdoms: Bacteria, Archaea, Protists, Plants, Fungi and Animals.

once.soru: Bacteria and archaea are both single-celled organisms with no nucleus. Are they in the same group?

secenekler.neden: Their cell walls and some of their molecules differ. By DNA, archaea are closer to eukaryotes than bacteria are.
Having no nucleus is a shared trait, but archaea are not bacteria.
Archaea are cellular organisms, not viruses.

cards.p: Bacteria and archaea are both single-celled prokaryotes. Bacteria have peptidoglycan in their cell walls, and archaea do not. Bacteria break down wastes, fix nitrogen and can cause disease. Archaea often live in extremely hot or salty places.

cards.p: Most protists are single-celled. The amoeba moves with false feet, and the paramecium moves with cilia. Euglena carries out photosynthesis in light and takes in ready-made food in the dark. Plasmodium causes malaria.
cards.key: Euglena can feed both as an autotroph and as a heterotroph.

once.soru: Euglena carries out photosynthesis in light and takes in ready-made food in the dark. Which kingdom is it in?

secenekler.neden: Euglena is a single-celled eukaryote. It does not belong to the plant or animal kingdom.
Euglena carries out photosynthesis, but it is single-celled and also takes in ready-made food. So it is not a plant.
Euglena takes in ready-made food, but it has chloroplasts. So it is not an animal.

cards.p: Most fungi are multicellular and made of threads called hyphae. Most break down dead remains. Yeast makes bread rise. A lichen is a fungus and an alga living together. The alga makes food, and the fungus protects the alga.

cards.key: A lichen is not a kingdom but a partnership between a fungus and an alga. Lichens are very sensitive to air pollution.

once.soru: Lichens that live on bare rock are actually a partnership of two organisms. Which two?

secenekler.neden: The alga makes food by photosynthesis. The fungus holds water and protects the alga.
A lichen is neither a plant nor an animal.
One partner can be a cyanobacterium, but the other is always a fungus.

cards.h: Why aren't viruses in any kingdom?
cards.p: As you saw in the first topic, viruses are not cells. Kingdoms were set up for cellular organisms. So viruses are not placed in any kingdom and are studied separately.

once.soru: Why aren't viruses placed in any kingdom?

secenekler.neden: Kingdoms were set up for cellular organisms. A virus is not a cell, so it is studied separately.
Bacteria are small too, but they belong to a kingdom. The test is being a cell, not size.
Being harmful is not a classification criterion.

cards.p:
• Science uses natural classification, based on relatedness.
• Moving down toward species, the number of species decreases, and shared traits and relatedness increase.
• Individuals that can produce fertile offspring belong to the same species. The mule is sterile.
• The binomial name is written in italics, and the genus starts with a capital letter.
• There are three domains and six kingdoms. Viruses are not in any kingdom.

quiz.q: Find where humans fit in classification. Match each level with the human group at that level.
quiz.e: Humans are in the animal kingdom, the chordate phylum, the mammal class, the primate order and the genus Homo. The species name is Homo sapiens.

quiz.q: Put each organism in its kingdom.
quiz.e: A cyanobacterium is a bacterium that carries out photosynthesis. The amoeba, euglena, paramecium and plasmodium are single-celled eukaryotic protists. Yeast, mold and mushrooms are in the fungus kingdom.

quiz.q: Match each term with its correct description.
ciftler: Those that can produce fertile offspring
First word of a binomial name
quiz.e: Individuals that can produce fertile offspring form a species, and the first word of a binomial name is the genus. Natural classification looks at relatedness, and artificial classification at appearance. The broadest level is the domain.

quiz.q: Which is an example of homologous organs?
o: A bird wing and a fly wing
A human arm and a whale flipper
A bat wing and a butterfly wing
A rose thorn and a hedgehog spine
quiz.e: A human arm and a whale flipper come from the same bone layout. Their origin is the same, but their jobs differ. Natural classification looks at similarities like this.
y: Both are for flying, but their origins differ. These are analogous organs.
Their jobs are the same, but their origins differ. This is a pair of analogous organs.
The plant's thorn and the animal's spine are only similar in job. Their origins are completely different.

hayvanlar-alemi.title: The animal kingdom: invertebrates and vertebrates
hayvanlar-alemi.summary: How do you tell the invertebrate phyla and vertebrate classes apart?

once.soru: An organism is multicellular, has no cell wall and takes in food by swallowing it. Which kingdom is it in?

secenekler.neden: Animals are multicellular, have no cell wall and are heterotrophs. They take in food by swallowing it.
Plants have a cellulose wall, and they carry out photosynthesis.
Fungi have a chitin wall. They digest food outside the body and absorb it.

cards.p: Vertebrates have a backbone made of vertebrae along their back, and it protects the spinal cord. Invertebrates have no backbone, but some of them have an exoskeleton. About 95% of animal species are invertebrates.

etk.soru: Put each animal in the right group.
ogeler: It has an internal skeleton of chalky plates under its skin, but no backbone.
It has well-developed eyes and a nervous system, but it is a mollusk and has no backbone.
Its skeleton is made of cartilage, but it has a backbone. It is a cartilaginous fish.
It looks like a fish, but it is a mammal and a vertebrate.

cards.p: Sponges have no true tissues. They feed by filtering food out of the water that flows through the pores in their body. Cnidarians such as jellyfish, corals and hydras have two cell layers and hunt with the stinging cells on their tentacles.

once.soru: A sponge passes water through the holes in its body. How does it get its food?

secenekler.neden: A sponge filters the food carried by the water that enters its pores. An adult sponge lives attached to one spot.
A sponge has no tentacles and no mouth.
Animals do not carry out photosynthesis.

cards.p: Flatworms have a flattened body, and most are parasites. Roundworms have a separate mouth and anus. The body of segmented worms is made of rings. They have a closed circulatory system, which means the blood always stays inside vessels.

once.soru: A tapeworm lives in the human intestine and has no digestive system. How does it feed?

secenekler.neden: A tapeworm absorbs the digested food in the intestine through its body surface. It is a parasitic flatworm.
A tapeworm does not suck blood. It absorbs the ready food in the intestine.
Animals do not carry out photosynthesis.

cards.p: Mollusks have a soft body. Most of them have a chalky shell made by the mantle. A snail's shell is one piece, while a mussel's shell has two parts. An octopus has no outer shell, and it is a very intelligent animal.

once.soru: Which one has no outer shell but is still a mollusk?

secenekler.neden: An octopus has no outer shell. It is an intelligent mollusk with well-developed eyes and a nervous system.
A snail has a one-piece shell.
A mussel has a two-part shell.

cards.p: The largest phylum is the arthropods. Their body is covered by an exoskeleton made of chitin, and they molt in order to grow. An insect has 3 pairs of legs, and a spider has 4 pairs. That is why a spider is not an insect.

cards.p: Echinoderms such as starfish and sea urchins live only in the sea. They have an internal skeleton made of chalky plates. The adults have radial symmetry and move with their tube feet.

once.soru: A starfish has an internal skeleton of chalky plates under its skin. Is a starfish a vertebrate?

secenekler.neden: A starfish has an internal skeleton, but no backbone. That is why it is an invertebrate.
Having an internal skeleton does not mean having a backbone.
A starfish larva has no backbone either.

cards.p: Fish breathe with gills and swim with fins. Their heart has two chambers, and their body temperature changes with the surroundings. A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, while an anchovy's skeleton is made of bone.

once.soru: How does a fish breathe in water?

secenekler.neden: Gills take up the oxygen dissolved in the water.
Most fish have no lungs. Fish breathe with gills.
Breathing through the skin matters for frogs. A fish breathes with gills.

cards.p: Amphibians such as frogs and salamanders lay eggs without shells in water. Their larvae are called tadpoles, and a tadpole breathes with gills. The tadpole goes through metamorphosis and turns into an adult with lungs. An amphibian's heart has three chambers.

once.soru: A tadpole, the young of a frog, breathes with gills in water. What does an adult frog breathe with?

secenekler.neden: The lungs develop during metamorphosis. An adult frog also breathes through its moist skin.
The gills disappear during metamorphosis.
An adult frog also has lungs. Breathing through the skin only helps them.

cards.p: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin. This reduces water loss. Reptiles breathe with lungs and lay shelled eggs on land. Most have a three-chambered heart, but a crocodile's heart has four chambers. Their body temperature changes with the surroundings.

cards.p: Feathers are found only in birds. Birds have hollow, light bones. They also have air sacs. Their heart has four chambers, and their body temperature is constant. Birds lay shelled eggs.

once.soru: A jellyfish has no brain, but when you touch it, its whole body reacts. What is its nervous system like?

secenekler.neden: In hydras and jellyfish, nerve cells spread through the body like a net. That is why a signal travels in every direction.
A brain and a spinal cord are found in vertebrates.
The animals with no nerve cells are sponges. A jellyfish has nerve cells.

cards.p:
• Animals are eukaryotic, multicellular and heterotrophic. Their cells have no wall.
• About 95% of species are invertebrates. The largest phylum is the arthropods.
• The heart has 2 chambers in fish, 3 in amphibians and most reptiles, and 4 in birds and mammals.
• Body temperature is constant only in birds and mammals.

quiz.q: Match each animal with its phylum.
quiz.e: A jellyfish is a cnidarian with stinging cells, a tapeworm is a flatworm, and a leech is a segmented worm. An octopus is a mollusk without a shell, and a starfish is an echinoderm.

quiz.q: Sort each animal by its body temperature.
quiz.e: Body temperature is constant only in birds and mammals. A penguin is a bird. A bat, a dolphin and a platypus are mammals. In fish, amphibians and reptiles, body temperature varies.

quiz.q: Match each set of features with its vertebrate class.
ciftler: Moist skin and lungs, three chambers
quiz.e: Gills and a two-chambered heart belong to fish, and moist skin and a three-chambered heart belong to amphibians. Dry scaly skin and shelled eggs belong to reptiles. Feathers are found only in birds, and hair and mammary glands only in mammals.

quiz.q: Which feature shows for certain that an animal is a vertebrate?
o: A closed circulatory system
A backbone made of vertebrae along its back
A skeleton that supports its body
Breathing with lungs
quiz.e: Earthworms and octopuses also have closed circulation. Arthropods have a skeleton too, in the form of an exoskeleton. Fish breathe with gills, not lungs. The feature that defines a vertebrate is the backbone.
y: Invertebrates such as the earthworm also have closed circulation. What sets vertebrates apart is the backbone.
An insect's exoskeleton also supports its body. What shows for certain that an animal is a vertebrate is a backbone made of vertebrae.
Fish are vertebrates, but they breathe with gills. The sure test is having a backbone.

bitkiler-alemi.title: The plant kingdom and plant groups
bitkiler-alemi.summary: Plant groups from mosses to flowering plants, alternation of generations, and monocots and dicots

cards.h: What makes a plant a plant
cards.p: Plants are eukaryotic and multicellular. Their cell walls are made of cellulose. They make food by photosynthesis and store the extra as starch. They protect their embryos inside a tissue.
